1059-the-world-set-free:
H. G. Wells imagines a world where scientists split the atom and give mankind limitless power, which kings and generals promptly use to wreck cities in a brief, dreadful war. From the ruins, survivors build a world state, end nations and war, and turn to peace. Wells wrote it in 1913, before any real atomic bomb.

The novel moves from labs and cabinets to ruined streets and a new order of reason. Its famous phrase, "atomic bomb," entered the language from these pages. The book reads as both warning and hope, and it shows Wells at his most prophetic about science and power.
10692-a-life-of-gen-robert-e-lee:
John Esten Cooke published A Life of Gen. Robert E. Lee in 1876, a few years after Lee's death, for Southern readers who honored him. The book opens with the Lees of Virginia and "Light-Horse Harry" Lee. It follows Robert Lee's youth at Stratford and his career in the United States Army, taking his mottoes on duty and calamity as its guide.

Later parts follow the Civil War in detail: the command before Richmond, the Chickahominy battles, and the campaigns that made Lee famous. Cooke writes as an admiring Virginian, not a neutral critic. Readers get a full, partisan life of the Confederate general, valuable as history and as a record of how the South remembered him.
10713-the-bullitt-mission-to-russia-test:
William C. Bullitt testified before the United States Senate Committee on Foreign Relations in 1919 about his mission to Russia, and this volume prints that testimony. Bullitt describes his official status, his orders, the Council of Ten's debate on Russia, the troops at Archangel, and the French blocking of a Prinkipo conference. His full report covers food, transport, armies, and Lenin's prestige.

The record also prints the projected Allied peace proposal, the breakfast with Lloyd George, and the suppression of Bullitt's report. It is a primary source on America's failed effort to settle with revolutionary Russia. Readers get diplomacy in the raw, from a witness who was there.
10976-the-apricot-tree:
A short moral tale published in 1851 by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, priced twopence, this book centres on a cottage near Ryefield village. An old woman reads her Bible by the window, her garden neat, her gooseberry bushes pruned, and an apricot tree against the cottage wall loaded with large, fine fruit. Tea, bread, and watercresses wait on a deal table.

Her grandson Ned learns kindness from his grandmother's teaching on coals of fire: gentleness can melt an enemy's heart. When Tom Andrews, a teasing boy whose father is out of work, goes hungry, Ned quietly shares half his dinner day after day. Tom at first takes the gift sulkily, then softens. The tale teaches children that steady kindness, not scolding, changes hearts.
11368-stories-of-inventors-the-adventure:
Russell Doubleday's 1904 Stories of Inventors collects true incidents and personal experiences of inventors and engineers for young readers. Chapters explain how Marconi telegraphs without wires, Santos-Dumont and his airship, how a fast train is run, how automobiles work. the fastest steamboats, life-savers and their apparatus, moving pictures, bridge builders, submarines, long-distance telephony, a thinking type-setting machine, and artificial ice-making.

Illustrations from Scientific American and other magazines accompany the text, including Marconi reading a message and Santos-Dumont rounding the Eiffel Tower. Doubleday writes with a boy's enthusiasm for machines. The book captures Edwardian faith in invention, when wireless, flight, and film all seemed newly possible.
12686-murder-in-any-degree:
Owen Johnson's 1913 collection, Murder in Any Degree, gathers nine stories first printed in magazines from 1906 to 1913. Titles run from Murder in Any Degree and One Hundred in the Dark through A Comedy for Wives, The Lie and Even Threes. A Man of No Imagination, Larry Moore, My Wife's Wedding Presents and The Surprises of the Lottery follow.

Illustrations by F. R. Gruger and Leon Guipon include a model offering to sit by the hour. Johnson, author of Stover at Yale, writes urbane, ironic tales of New York society, crime and marriage. The collection shows a popular Edwardian storyteller at ease with twist, wit and moral surprise.
1348-a-master-s-degree:
Margaret Hill McCarter dedicates this novel to Kansas boys and girls who have not yet earned their degrees, and to older folk chasing a larger mastery of life. Its hero, Vic Burleigh, arrives at Sunrise College, where Dean Funnybone greets him and a keen young professor becomes his rival from the first day.

Through study, work, and plain duty, Vic learns that a true master's degree is won by character rather than by papers alone. The book is earnest and warm, written to stir young readers toward steady effort. It reads as a moral tale of college, home, and growing up in Kansas.
1394-the-holly-tree:
Told in three branches, this Christmas book opens with a bashful narrator who keeps one secret all his life: his own shyness. Snowbound at an inn under the sign of the holly tree, he listens to fellow travellers and recalls his own past, from a boyhood mishap to a grown man's awkward loves.

The branches move between confession, anecdote, and ghostly fancy, all in a warm fireside voice. The humour is self-mocking and the feeling is kind. It is a small, charming seasonal book about timid people, chance meetings, and the stories strangers tell on a winter night.
15960-literary-character-of-men-of-geniu:
A study of genius by Isaac Disraeli, in a new edition edited by his son, the Earl of Beaconsfield. Frederick Warne and Company issued it in London in 1850, printed by Bradbury, Agnew. Disraeli draws literary character from men's own feelings and confessions, not from gossip alone. His preface states the method plainly.

Poets, scholars, and writers speak for themselves across the chapters, in letters, diaries, and laments. Ambition, melancholy, pride, and industry recur as marks of the literary temper. Disraeli writes with wit and wide reading. The book still interests students of authorship: genius seen from inside, by a man who knew writers well.
17856-prisoners-of-chance-the-story-of-w:
Randall Parrish wrote this romance of Geoffrey Benteen, borderman, and his love for a lady of France. Parrish also wrote When Wilderness Was King and Bob Hampton of Placer. It was published in Chicago in 1908 by A. C. McClurg and Company, with full-colour pictures by the Kinneys. A frontispiece shows the hero clasping the lady's hands in a broken farewell.

Chapters open with a request for aid, a perilous venture, and a visit to the flagship. A council of war, the deck of the Santa Maria, and the role of Pere Cassati follow, with the Chevalier de Noyan and favoured of the gods ahead. Readers get a swashbuckling romance of the French frontier, in Parrish's sturdy style.
17999-the-chief-legatee:
Anna Katharine Green wrote The Chief Legatee in 1906, printed in New York and London with water-color pictures by Frank T. Merrill. Green, famed for The Leavenworth Case, was one of America's first great mystery writers, and this book shows her at her intricate best.

Part one, A Woman of Mystery, opens with a bride of five hours, a lady in number three, and a lawyer who waits. Wills, heirs, and hidden words drive the plot, as Green sorts true claimants from false. It is a long, clever puzzle novel, best for readers who like wills, secrets, and a slow, careful untying of knots.
18207-coffee-and-repartee:
John Kendrick Bangs wrote Coffee and Repartee in 1899, printed in New York and London by Harper and Brothers, in the Black and White series. Bangs, a humorist of the day, gives short, sharp talk over coffee, in the style of a New York club.

The book's title piece asks, are you related to Governor McKinley, and the talk runs from politics to letters with quick, comic thrusts. Bangs writes with the light, topical wit of the 1890s press. It is a small, funny book of table talk, best for readers who like old American humor in short, bright bites.
18662-the-tale-of-buster-bumblebee:
Arthur Scott Bailey wrote this Tuck-Me-In Tale in 1918, with pictures by Harry L. Smith. It follows Buster Bumblebee from a big family of at least two hundred living in an old meadow house. Chirpy Cricket gives advice, old Mr. Crow comes to the rescue, and Johnnie Green gets stung, while a robber fly, a carpenter bee, and a drone cross Buster's path.

Later chapters bring a speech, a feast at Farmer Green's, a bumblebee in a pumpkin, and games played on old dog Spot. Bailey mixes bee lore with gentle jokes in short chapters. Young readers get a buzzing woodland tale with a boastful but likable hero.
19111-code-three:
Rick Raphael wrote this science fiction tale, first printed in Analog in February 1963. Cars on fast highways travel in lines, watched by the highway police of tomorrow, in cruisers as different as the roads themselves. Patrol Sergeant Ben Martin steps out of the Philadelphia Barracks into cold wind and coming snow.

Martin and his young partner Ferguson face painting crews, rerouted traffic, and a priority Army missile convoy of thirty-four units moving at green lane speeds that night. Light snow may turn to ice rain. Readers get a brisk future police story of roads, weather, and duty.
19191-the-fruit-of-the-tree:
Edith Wharton wrote this 1907 novel about industry, medicine, and moral choice at a New England mill town. In the surgical ward at Hanaford, nurse Justine Brent tends Dillon, a mill hand whose injured arm may be lost. Amherst, a reform-minded manager, presses her on the case and on the lack of an emergency hospital at the mills.

Dillon's wife, worn by cotton dust at twenty-six yet looking forty, and their three children sharpen the moral stakes. Love, duty, and the cost of reform tangle as Amherst and Justine weigh action against mercy. Readers get a powerful Wharton novel on work, wealth, and conscience.
19406-scientific-american-volume-xxxvi-n:
The February 24, 1877 number of Scientific American was a weekly journal. It covered useful knowledge across art, science, mechanics, chemistry, and making things. Munn and Company of Park Row, New York, edited it. Contents open with engineering and mechanics, including artificial production of ice by steam. The paper cost three dollars and twenty cents a year.

A long piece on the date palm calls it the most important of its genus. It shoots to eighty feet with a crown of pinnated leaves. It bears after six to ten years and stays fruitful for over two hundred years. It yields one to four hundredweight a season. Readers get a vivid Victorian science weekly, practical and curious.
19510-north-of-fifty-three:
Bertrand W. Sinclair wrote this northern adventure novel, put out in New York in the mid nineteen teens with pictures by Anton Otto Fischer. A lady and two gentlemen meet in the Cariboo country, where wills, gold, and a long trail to a Hudson's Bay post test every claim.

Hazel, a spirited young woman with a pony and a camp outfit, refuses to vanish into the background of a man's tale. The novel mixes romance with the hard facts of northern travel: distance, weather, and the need for a preacher at the end of a long road.
19776-the-ordeal-a-mountain-romance-of-t:
Charles Egbert Craddock was the pen name of Mary Noailles Murfree. The Ordeal is her mountain romance of Tennessee. It opens in the Great Smoky Mountains after the springs hotel has closed. The Briscoe family lingers too long at their summer cottage, neighbors think. The hotel guests and staff have all vanished townward. Solitude there turns sharp enough to foster fear.

Murfree made the Tennessee mountains famous in fiction. Her dialect and scenery set the standard for Appalachian local color. Isolation drives her plots: weather, kin, and old feuds close in. The Ordeal works that pattern in romance form. Readers get the Smokies before the national park existed. Her mountains are wilder and lonelier than today's.
20091-no-surrender-a-tale-of-the-rising-:
G. A. Henty wrote No Surrender, a tale of the rising in La Vendée, in France. The Vendée rose against the French Revolution in a fierce civil war. Thick woods, called the Bocage, covered much of that region. Such ground should have helped local fighters who knew each lane.

Yet, Henty notes, the rebels fought most big battles in open ground. There, trained troops held the edge over brave but raw bands. His tale follows young heroes caught in that doomed, brave rising. Readers get Henty's blend of true war history and boys' adventure at full stretch.
20449-the-plum-tree:
David Graham Phillips published The Plum Tree in 1905, a novel about the spoils of American politics. In the slang of the time, plums were the jobs and favors a winning party handed out. The story follows a man drawn into that system of power.

The narrator recalls his young wife at their scant breakfast table. He was as blue as ever a man of twenty-five could be, while she stayed brave and confident. Her courage, he says, was no pretense meant to cheer him. Phillips builds his tale of ambition and corruption on such home scenes.
20628-torchy-and-vee:
Sewell Ford's Torchy and Vee, published in 1918, marries off his red-headed office hero at last. Vee is the stenographer Torchy courted through the earlier books. Now they keep house together, and Torchy narrates married life in his unstoppable slang.

He looks forward to enjoying a little family reunion. Vee will tell him how she has been getting along, and what cute tricks young Master Richard has developed while he was gone. But right in the midst of the domestic sketch, Vee breaks loose with news of her own. Ford keeps the office comedy running at home.
20909-under-the-tree:
A shadow slips across the ground, and a child looks up to the sky in Under the Tree. It hangs on the poplar, jerks, then creeps away and will not stay. Elizabeth Madox Roberts writes as if some chain pulls it from the top.

Roberts's 1922 poems catch the world as a small child sees and names it. Trees, clouds, and beasts take on fresh, strange life in her lines. She wrote from Kentucky with a child's eye and a poet's ear, in a small classic of childhood verse. The book is a small book of verse for the young.
21051-skylark-three:
Liberties with sound science are owned up front in Skylark Three, with a frank caveat. Some theories used here its author holds sound, some unsound, and some beyond his line. E. E. Smith asks readers to grant that mix as the tale's base.

Richard Seaton and his crew ride the vast Skylark Three among alien worlds. Fenachrone foes, space fleets, and wonders of scale fill Smith's sequel. His Lensman-age craft of piling marvel on marvel runs at full tilt here. Readers who crave old, huge space opera will find Skylark Three a rich, breathless feast of it.
21103-sisters-three:
Norah, Lettice, and Hilary are sisters growing up in England's Lake District, daughters of a well-known author. Mrs George de Horne Vaizey opens on New Year's Day, with the girls sighing for something nice to happen amid practising, housework, and classes. Change comes when one sister reaches marriageable age.

She chooses among eligible young men, and the wedding plans advance a long way. Then she realises she cannot go through with it. Around that crisis Vaizey draws daily life for young women around 1900, down to judging young men by their moustaches. The tale stays light even when hearts are at stake.
21883-we-three:
A man plans his winters around a woman he must not meet in Gouverneur Morris's We Three, published in 1916. If Lucy Fulton goes to Palm Beach, he will go to Aiken; if she goes to Newport, he will take Bar Harbor. They have been asked not to meet, he says, and will do so only by accident. Then he starts again at the beginning, with a small boy warned against matches.

That boy played with matches anyway and never burned anything down, which is his parable for the tale. Morris builds a society romance on restraint: two people, a promise, and a third life between them. Henry Hutt's pictures show Lucy dark against a lit hall. The voice is dry, rueful, and very much of its wealthy world.
21934-the-gold-of-fairnilee:
Fairy gold glitters under a Scottish Border house in Andrew Lang's The Gold of Fairnilee. Lang made the tale for a child far away in Australia. Lang tells his niece Jeanie that he and her father dug for treasure as boys in the Camp of Rink, and found none. The story, he promises, will tell her why. Randal of Fairnilee lives three hundred sixty years before the reader, in a high house with pepperbox towers.

His father is gone to the wars, and Randal lives with his mother, old nurse Nancy, and Simon Grieve the butler. Fairies, a hidden hoard, and the Flodden sorrow of Scotland weave through the tale. Lang mixes history and fairy lore in his tenderest manner. It is his own favorite among his tales for children.
21956-report-of-the-knaresbrough-rail-wa:
A canal that became a railway is argued for in this 1820 report of the Knaresborough Rail-Way Committee in Yorkshire. In March 1818 the town's meeting authorized a survey for the most eligible line, at first for a canal. The report addresses the noblemen, gentlemen, and subscribers on the adopted line with due deference. The Nidd valley, it notes, turns sixty-seven mills with its falls.

The committee pleads that hostile landlords, poor soil, or weak trade might once have killed the project, but none of these now applies. Knaresborough's slow progress beside other towns is held up as the shame to cure. The pamphlet is a fossil of the railway age's birth: local pride, water power, and a surveyor's line offered to an enlightened and liberal public.
22236-flag-of-the-free:
Flag of the Free is a slim volume of patriotic verse published in 1917, the year America entered the Great War. Its title poem addresses the flag directly. Bright beacon of the azure sky, the poet calls it, true light of freedom's dome. The poem prays that the flag will shine until all nations cease to grope in vain for liberty.

Such verse flooded American print in 1917 and 1918. Schools, newspapers, and war meetings all wanted poems that schoolchildren could recite and crowds could cheer. Flag of the Free is a surviving sample of that home-front poetry. It shows how the flag's cult looked in print at the moment of America's first great crusade abroad.
22354-the-adventures-of-maya-the-bee:
Waldemar Bonsels wrote The Adventures of Maya the Bee, published in English in 1922. Maya is a baby bee waking to life in the hive. An elderly lady-bee named Cassandra helps her slip from her cell.

Cassandra commands great respect among the bees. Those were exciting days in the bee nation, Bonsels writes. A rebellion had broken out that the queen could not suppress. Maya thus enters a hive already in turmoil and change. Her adventures carry young readers through the insect world. The story mixes nature lore with a small heroine's curiosity. It became a lasting favorite of children's literature in many lands.
2323-recollections-and-letters-of-genera:
Captain Robert E. Lee, the general's son, gathers his father's letters and his own memories in this intimate portrait. Recollections and Letters shows Lee at home and at war: writing to family, managing Arlington, and bearing defeat with the dignity that made him a legend in the South. The letters reveal a private man behind the marble image.

The volume's value lies in its firsthand detail, from camp life to postwar Lexington. Its view is sympathetic, as a son's memoir must be, and readers should weigh it against fuller histories. For Civil War students, it remains a key source.
23584-the-gold-of-chickaree:
Susan Warner and Anna Warner wrote this eighteen seventy six novel, a continuation of Wych Hazel, in Putnam's edition. The Atlantic Monthly, reviewing it in March eighteen seventy seven, found Wych Hazel rich and pert. Her lover Rollo, Dane, Duke, or Olaf by turns is rich and masterful, and the pair's sudden marriage is the heart of this sequel.

Critics of the day sparred over the book, with some scorning mere denunciation and others crying out against books without truth or beauty. The Warners write a domestic romance of wealth, pride, and love, in the sentimental style that filled Victorian parlours. Readers of period fiction will find a full sample of that world, where a heroine's wit and a hero's will clash and join in a marriage plot.
23767-the-talkative-tree:
H. B. Fyfe's The Talkative Tree opens with a crash landing on a small, murky planet. The pilot of the Peace State brings her down as well as anyone could, given an obscure star, a damaged stellar drive, and an atmosphere that defies precision scanners. Steward Peter Kolin admits the casualties might have been far worse.

Chief Steward Slichow volunteers his section for scouting, hunting for natural foods near the steaming hull. The planet belongs to the service of Haurtoz, fifteen light-years from Earth, where loyalty is strictly kept. Its vines, as the opening warns, have no manners — but what can you expect, when they used to be men?
23923-how-doth-the-simple-spelling-bee:
Owen Wister, author of The Virginian, published How Doth the Simple Spelling Bee with Macmillan in 1907, with pictures by F. R. Gruger. Its title parodies Watts, How doth the little busy bee improve each shining hour, and its subject is the spelling reform agitation of the day.

The narrator, working on an index, receives printed cards asking Why Heifer, then Why not Heffer, and tosses both into his waste-paper basket. Professors Totts and Egghorn, Masticator B. Fellows, and Professor Dudelsacker carry the comic war over spelling into learned absurdity. Wister's satire stings the reformers while laughing at the language they would mend.
26054-a-color-notation-a-measured-color-:
A. H. Munsell sets out a measured system for naming and matching colors, built on three qualities he calls hue, value, and chroma. His color sphere places each shade by its place on that solid, so that teachers and students can speak of a color in exact terms instead of loose names. Models, charts, and a course of study carry the reader from simple scales to full color balance.

The text moves through prismatic colors and the pigment color sphere, stressing balance over strong or crude hues. Munsell warns that violent colors harm taste, and he argues that harmony comes from keeping colors in balance within the sphere rather than pushing toward extremes. Lectures first given to art students and teachers form the base of the lessons, which end with practical work in matching and arranging color.
26344-letters-of-a-dakota-divorcee:
Jane Burr's Letters of a Dakota Divorcee, issued at Boston in 1909 and dedicated to her Sioux Falls friends, satirizes the divorce colony era in letters. Its author's note treats the divorcee as a species. Once she matured in three short months in South Dakota. A referendum requiring a full year drove herds onward to Nevada and Oklahoma, where the climate suited her better.

Letters gossip about Alice Noah, who takes legal separation papers in New York, and about alimony, snobbery, and tradespeople branded to the third generation. Burr jokes about sentimental tramways and moral funds, and about a girl cinching alimony until she finds another match. The book offers a sharp, funny view of marriage law as a western industry.
26526-stingaree:
E. W. Hornung's 1905 collection, illustrated by George W. Lambert, follows Stingaree, the gentleman bushranger of the Australian bush. A voice in the wilderness opens the book, where Hilda Bouverie, singing at the piano, stops on a high note at a step outside. Later tales take in the black hole of Glenranald, a bushranger at bay, the taking of Stingaree, and the honor of the road.

Stingaree's code and charm carry the stories, from the purification of Mulfera to a duel in the desert and the moth and the star. He sings Gilbert and Sullivan airs and insists, despite temptations to belong to other nations, that he remains an Englishman. Hornung, creator of Raffles, gives the outlaw the same polish and daring.
26912-report-of-the-juvenile-delinquency:
A 1955 report laid on the table of New Zealand's House of Representatives, printed by authority at Wellington under chairman the Honorable R. M. Algie. A special select committee of ten members was appointed on September 28, 1954. Six were named by the Prime Minister and four by the Leader of the Opposition. Its charge was the Mazengarb Committee's report on moral delinquency in children and adolescents, with recommendations or observations to follow.

Time ran short twice, and the House extended the deadline first to September 1, 1955, then to October 1. The committee met twice during recess and on several occasions during the session, but it did not rehear the Mazengarb evidence or deal broadly with the causes of delinquency and their remedies. Its business was narrower: study the legislation, weigh each Mazengarb recommendation, and set out excerpts, including police material on the selection and training of policewomen.
27920-ben-comee:
M. J. Canavan wrote Ben Comee, a tale of Rogers's Rangers in 1758 and 1759, published by Macmillan in 1899 and reprinted often through 1916. Ben is born in Lexington in 1737, traps muskrats, hunts foxes, and is apprenticed before joining Rogers's Rangers and marching west to war.

Chapters follow fights with French and Indians, Fort Ticonderoga, the fight at Fort Anne, trapping bob-cats, a winter scouting expedition, and the attack on the St. Francis Indians. The novel gives young readers a vivid, boy-centered view of the French and Indian War on the frontier.
28500-all-about-coffee:
William H. Ukers, editor of The Tea and Coffee Trade Journal, wrote All About Coffee, published in New York in 1922. The volume opens with a coffee thesaurus and a picture of the bean's path from plantation to cup. Early chapters treat the word's origin, the plant's history, and the first centuries of coffee drinking.

Later chapters follow coffee into France, England, Holland, and Germany, naming first coffee houses, traders, and auctions. A first public auction at Amsterdam in 1711 saw Java coffee bring forty-seven cents a pound, green. Readers get a full reference work on growing, trade, custom, and the drink itself.
28656-typee:
Herman Melville's early novel tells of a sailor who deserts his whaling ship in the Marquesas Islands of the South Pacific. With his shipmate Toby, the narrator escapes into the mountains of Nukuheva and comes down into the valley of the Typee people, whose name other sailors speak with fear. He stays among them for weeks, eating, bathing, and watching their daily life.

The book mixes travel writing with invention, describing island customs, food, tattooing, and the valley's beauty while the narrator wonders whether he is a guest or a prisoner. Published before Moby-Dick, it made Melville's name and still reads as a vivid account of first contact between a lone European sailor and a Pacific island society. Its questions about freedom and civilization run through the whole tale.
28683-the-roof-tree:
Charles Neville Buck's The Roof Tree, published by Doubleday, Page and Company of Garden City and Toronto in 1921, opens in a mountain cabin after a pistol shot. Between smoke-darkened walls the echo lingers, a man stares at the pistol on the floor, and a woman clutches her thin bosom. Her husband lies on the puncheon floor, shot at nearly touching range.

Illustrations promise a girl slender and upright as a birch, an old tree with a spell to bewitch folks, and Bas Rowlett keyed for an ordeal. The mountain feud, the roof tree itself, and love under threat drive the novel. Readers get a Kentucky mountain tale of violence, loyalty, and reckoning.
29290-now-we-are-three:
Joe L. Hensley, an attorney in Madison, Indiana, wrote this science fiction story about the age of bomb testing. John Rush, who has quit the work, still feels guilty. He has seen guilt in his wife's eyes and in the eyes of others. At home he tucks covers around his wife Mary, whose breathing is smooth and easy, almost as if she were sleeping.

Beside them move the twins, their smooth hands following his, their blind eyes intent on nothingness. Hensley asks where the world is going when bombs have been tested to the finite degree. Readers get a challenging, somber story about responsibility, family, and a tomorrow shaped by weapons tested too far.
29601-see:
Edward G. Robles, Jr.'s short tale opens with a hobo waking on Skid Row, broke, jeans empty, nursing a massive hangover. He resolves to make a man of himself or else, and the tale's tag line warns: seeing things? Skip the analyst and see the Commission, if it does not find you first. Dirty Pete, the tale says, found the thing no one could get rid of.

Robles draws a sharp line between hobo, tramp, and bum: the hobo works and moves on, the tramp mooches and moves on, and the bum mooches and hangs around. His hobos call themselves aristocrats. Fans of pulp science fiction will enjoy a wry, streetwise tale of visions, commissions, and men on the move.
30439-mrs-tree:
Laura E. Richards writes Mrs. Tree, copyrighted in 1902 and published in Boston that June, with chapters that trace wedding bells, Phoebe's opinions, and the arrival of Tommy Candy and Solomon, his grandfather. Old friends, a new postmaster, Miss Penny's shop, and tea and garden parties fill the middle of the book.

Later chapters follow Mr. Butters discoursing, Miss Phoebe passing on, a peak in Darien, life in death, and a letter brought by Tommy Candy. Maria and Doctor Stedman's patient close the named scenes. Richards, author of Captain January and Melody, writes a warm domestic novel of village life, kinship, and quiet change.
31056-the-grandee:
Armando Palacio Valdés's novel The Grandee, translated from the Spanish by Rachel Challice and published in London by William Heinemann in 1894, appeared as number sixteen in Heinemann's International Library. Edmund Gosse edited the series. Fifteen chapters follow the grandee's house, a discovery, the town, a love story, the jokes of Paco Gomez, the señoritas de Meré, and a masquerade. Five years after, they bring rage, justice, martyrdom, and capitulation.

The novel mixes provincial Spanish society, romance, and satire, with a large household and a small town watching every move. In Challice's translation, English readers get a lively, clear-eyed Spanish tale of pride, passion, and the slow settling of accounts.
31831-marcy-the-refugee:
Harry Castlemon's Marcy, the Refugee was published at Philadelphia by Porter and Coates in 1892 as part of Castlemon's War Series. It takes up once more the Union hero Marcy Gray, a North Carolina boy who tried hard and unsuccessfully to be true to his colors. In his small schooner Fairy Belle, Marcy had ferried his brother Sailor Jack to the Federal blockading fleet for Jack to join the navy.

Chapters follow Beardsley's homecoming, neighborhood gossip, Marcy's rash wish and its gratification, the arrival of the fleet, a search for a pilot, and Marcy in action. Readers get a boys' Civil War adventure of divided loyalties on the Carolina coast, where a loyal boy risks being shot by both sides.
32559-adventures-of-hans-sterk-the-south:
Captain A. W. Drayson's Adventures of Hans Sterk opens with an extraordinary emigration from the Cape of Good Hope in 1835. Nearly six thousand souls left without guides or clear knowledge of where they were going. They placed all in the lottery of the wilderness to escape what they saw as oppression and to build a free nation of their own in Africa's interior.

Soon after leaving the Cape, the emigrants were attacked by the chief of a powerful Matabili tribe, into whose country they had trespassed, and fought severe battles against overwhelming numbers, generally winning. A party then pushed east toward Natal, where a Zulu chief named Dingaan treacherously massacred them. Drayson, a Royal Artillery captain, writes a Victorian hunter's tale of trek, battle, and frontier life.
3263-the-portygee:
Joseph C Lincoln opens this Cape Cod tale in a December storm. Clouds cloak the sky in a ragged cloak, and stars shine through holes only to vanish as cloud tatters hurry across. Pines thresh on the hilltops, bare wild-cherry and silverleaf branches scrape and rattle, and a raw, wet, salty wind tears in from the sea over the dunes.

The Portygee of the title is the Portuguese Cape Codder at the story's center. Lincoln, master of the Cape's speech and temper, builds his novel from such weather and such folk. Storms, boats, and neighbors whose pride and kindness are tested by the sea carry a plain coastal tale.
33531-the-subspecies-of-the-mountain-chi:
Joseph Grinnell studies the geographic variation of the mountain chickadee in this 1918 University of California publication in zoology. Fieldwork by the Museum of Vertebrate Zoology in the Inyo region of eastern California in 1917 drew his attention to chickadees that looked paler and longer-tailed than birds from the Sierras. To judge those differences, he assembled material from across the species' range.

The study rests on 464 skins drawn from the national museum, the Biological Survey, and several private collections. Grinnell compares plumage and measurements, defines the subspecies, and illustrates the account with three figures. It is a careful early example of museum-based taxonomy, showing how field collecting and comparative series turn small regional differences into named forms.
34263-the-banshee:
The Banshee, by Elliot O'Donnell, came out at London and Edinburgh from Sands and Company. O'Donnell had written on haunted places in England and on years spent as a ghost hunter. He calls the banshee a ghost that fits wild, fair Ireland, its home ground.

The name, he says, comes from the Irish Bean Sidhe, read as a woman of the fairy race, or a lady of death. It is a family ghost, tied to old Irish lines, and stays with them in fall as in rise. Thirteen chapters treat banshees of past times, cruel banshees, and banshees abroad. More treat banshees on fields of war, at sea, and in Scotland. The last gives the author and his own stark meetings. Ghost fans get a full store of lore and tales.
37357-annie-o-the-banks-o-dee:
Gordon Stables wrote Annie o' the Banks o' Dee, issued in London in an edition dated 1899. The first chapter, At Bilberry Hall, opens with lines of an old song. The singer calls Annie the sweetest lass to him, a gem that would have thrown lustre over a jewelled crown. Far up the romantic Dee, almost hidden by dark spruce and firs, stands the old mansion-house of Bilberry Hall.

A castle it had been in the brave days of old, many-gabled and turreted. It once belonged to Gordons, stripped of house and lands after Culloden, when the Bloody Duke's soldiery laid waste Badenoch. But Bilberry Hall is quiet now after sunset. Only the low moan of wind in the forest and the murmur of the river break the stillness. At such an hour Laird McLeod summons the servants, sets the big hall Bible before him, and reads aloud.
38516-the-children-s-life-of-the-bee:
Maurice Maeterlinck life of the bee stands here cut for children. Sutro and Williams selected and arranged the text for young readers. Dodd, Mead printed it in New York in 1919, Detmold plates. Contents open on the threshold of the hive, then the swarm.

The foundation of the city and the young queens follow next. The massacre of the males and progress of the race close it. The author first saw an apiary in Dutch Flanders long ago. An old thinker there had built his hives among bright flowers. A sphinx plate and a queen taking possession with her court stand in the list.
39231-joel-a-boy-of-galilee:
Joel: A Boy of Galilee is a book for the young by Annie Fellows Johnston. Her great set of the small chief tales is list at the front at length. Each book of that set is bound in cloth with plates. The set is sold as a whole in a box as well. Small forms of the set, at a low price, stand in a next list.

More sets of the same hand stand past those lists. A snug nook set of thin books, a set of feast day forms in hue, and more tales of boys and beasts fill the front pages. The tale of this book is set in the land of the great book of faith. Its hero is a boy of the lake shire of that land.
39248-nuova-or-the-new-bee:
Vernon Kellogg tells a bee's life in Nuova, or The New Bee, a story for children of five to fifty, published at Boston and New York in 1920. Charlotte Kellogg wrote the songs and Milo Winter the pictures. His prefatory note admits that most of the bee matter is true, and that the likeness to human social movements is the book's moral. A pronunciation list gives the Italian names of the bees.

Nuova wakes gradually into the hive, works as nurse, meets the bee moth and Beffa, and joins Hero in the birth of the Princess. Later chapters take her outside, into battle, a great courting chase and a beautiful garden.
40674-sawn-off-a-tale-of-a-family-tree:
George Manville Fenn wrote Sawn Off, a Tale of a Family Tree, in an edition dated 1891. Doctor Salado and his daughter Very open the tale at a breakfast room window in high dudgeon. Overnight, hands have raised a hoarding fifty feet long and twenty feet high right across the road from their cottage.

The boards cut off their view of park and manor house down a fine oak vista. Salado calls it a planned insult by my lord and his sly agent, and longs for an axe, though Very stays his swearing with a small hand. Placards for an auction go up as they watch. Naboth and his vineyard heads the chapter, a fit sign for a tale of spite, land, and proud kin.
40836-the-mysterious-three:
The Mysterious Three is a mystery novel by William Le Queux. It opens in the hall of Sir Charles Thorold, who asks his wife abruptly if she knows a Mr Smithson. Lady Thorold, pouring tea, says she does not. Thorold turns to the butler, who reports that the man asked to see either master or mistress.

The visitor was tall and powerfully built, and came in a car. Vera Thorold, the couple's only child, listens with twinkling eyes; she has a rare sense of humour. The unanswered call sets the mystery going. Le Queux wrote shelf-loads of such tales of secrets, spies, and country-house intrigue for the readers of his day.
40850-carolina-lee:
Lilian Bell wrote Carolina Lee, a novel copyrighted in 1906 and issued at New York in 1907 with a colour frontispiece by Dora Wheeler Keith. Bell had written Hope Loring and At Home with the Jardines before it. The heroine was born in Paris, a fact the ardent little American girl treats as something to live down. Asked where she was born, she answers that she is named for an American state.

Her father holds that they are Americans first and Southerners second. The chapters move from Captain Winchester Lee and a first grief through a trial of faith to Whitehall, Guildford, and kinfolk. A blind baby, letters from Carolina and from Kate, and a house party fill the middle of the tale before loose threads are tied.
4098-on-the-trail-of-grant-and-lee:
Frederick Trevor Hill's book follows the trails of Ulysses S. Grant and Robert E. Lee through the Civil War. A sampled letter shows Lee writing to his old commander Scott from Arlington on April 20, 1861, tendering his resignation after their interview two days before.

Lee writes that the parting cost him deeply, and that he would have resigned at once but for the struggle it caused him. Hill builds the two generals' stories from letters, marches, and battlefields. Readers who like Civil War biography told through documents will find a clear, human account of rivals bound by war.
41002-if-sinners-entice-thee:
If Sinners Entice Thee is a novel of gambling and honour by William Le Queux. Chapter one opens in a shabby little dining room in a sleepy English village. Zertho, a tall dark bearded man of about forty, presses a proposal there. Captain Erle Brooker, his host, refuses it flatly on his daughter's account.

Zertho wants Liane Brooker made Princess d'Auzac, and mocks her father's scruples as sentiment. The two men ran a snug little gambling place at Nice for five years. Brooker quit rather than fleece beardless boys at the tables any longer. Liane, he says, brings him luck and once prompted his last great coup. Her advice broke the partnership, and Zertho sneers at a mere girl's counsel. Brooker holds that he will never trade his child's happiness for gain.
42831-love-in-a-cloud-a-comedy-in-filigr:
Arlo Bates wrote Love in a Cloud, a comedy in filigree, published at Boston and New York in 1900. Twenty-eight chapters bear matching titles in threes and fours. The Mischief of a Maid opens it, then The Madness of a Man and The Babble of a Tea.

The Tickling of an Author, the Blazing of Rank, and the Mischief of a Widow follow. The Counsel of a Mother, the Test of Love, the Business of a Clubman, and the Game of Cross-Purposes fill the pattern. Later come the Mischief of a Letter, of a Gentleman, of Men, of a Fiancé, and of a Cad. The Waking of a Spinster and the Wooing of a Widow near the Climax of Comedy. Readers get a society novel built like a dance, all pattern and sparkle.
4307-in-the-year-of-jubilee:
George Gissing set this novel in the year of Queen Victoria's jubilee, opening on a Sunday morning in Camberwell. Arthur Peachey slips out of his double-fronted house in De Crespigny Park for a summer holiday, his first since his marriage three years before. The street, with its trees and stucco pillars, looks pleasant to a suburban eye.

The story follows Peachey and Miss Lord through a London celebrating its queen, while private lives run their own course. Gissing uses the jubilee year as a backdrop for courtship, money, and class. The novel shows his gift for making a particular London year feel lived in, street by street.
43606-sport-in-abyssinia-or-the-mareb-an:
The Earl of Mayo, a lieutenant in the Grenadier Guards, wrote of sport in Abyssinia in a book printed in London in 1876. A photo of the party fronts the book. Mayo says he gives a plain account of what he did and saw, from his notes and daily journal. Tales in it were told by natives and Europeans round camp fires and on long marches.

The Mareb and Tackazzee rivers name his hunting ground. Pick a back rides, vulture traps, a baggage train, convict labour, and a Turkish dinner party fill the contents. Place names are spelt as they are pronounced, he notes. Mayo hoped to return under better luck, and his book keeps the rough charm of a young officer's safari.
43624-my-friend-annabel-lee:
My Friend Annabel Lee, by Mary MacLane, was published at Chicago in 1903. Stone and Company issued it in September of that year for the author. A portrait and signature of MacLane stand in the front of the book. The coming of Annabel Lee opens the contents at page one.

The flat surfaces of things and My Friend Annabel Lee follow in the contents. Boston, a small house in the country, and the half conscious soul fill the next heads. The young books of Trowbridge and a song of three grains of corn come after. Minnie Maddern Fiske gets a chapter of theatre talk in the list. The Montana diarist who startled 1902 turns to an imagined friend in this second book.
43946-the-sea-beach-at-ebb-tide-a-guide-:
Augusta Foote Arnold's The Sea-Beach at Ebb-Tide, published by the Century Company in New York in nineteen one, guides the study of seaweeds and lower shore animals. More than six hundred illustrations support the promise of its subtitle, a guide to life found between tide-marks. Early chapters teach signs on the beach, collecting, and classification, with notes on how shore life spreads through the sea.

The main parts divide the shore by kind. Marine algae come first, sorted into blue-green, grass-green, brown, and red seaweeds, with a chapter on collecting at Bar Harbor. Marine invertebrates follow, from sponges and polyps to worms. A Shakespeare line about desperate studies stands as the book's motto.
43995-peter-parley-s-visit-to-london-dur:
Peter Parley came to London for the crowning of Queen Victoria, in a child's book printed there in 1839. He gives the pages to the good little boys and girls of Great Britain. A plate shows the coronation itself. Eleven chapters carry the tour.

Parley lands, views the new crown, and walks Westminster Abbey and Hyde Park. Tales of the queen fill two chapters. The abbey on coronation morning and the tale of Saint Edward's Chair follow. The ride to the abbey and the rite itself take the middle. Lights, fire works, and a review in Hyde Park close the book. The old man's plain talk made big state rites clear to young readers of the day.
44317-the-bungalow-boys-north-of-fifty-t:
Dexter J Forrester sends his boys into the far north in The Bungalow Boys North of Fifty-Three, published in New York in 1914 with pictures by Charles L Wrenn. A front plate shows the two Dacre boys hauling their chum Sandy out of a tight spot. The contents promise a trapper's hut, a friendly Indian, wolves, and a fight to the death with The Wolf.

The tale opens on the ice-fast Porcupine River in the Frying Pan Range, where a small steamer lies frozen in for the winter. Snow slides from the birch boughs and no bird sings. Boys who like snow, dogs, and peril will march gladly.
4511-the-life-of-the-bee:
Maurice Maeterlinck wrote this study of bees, translated by Alfred Sutro and published in New York in 1914, after its first appearance in 1901. He states at once that he does not intend a treatise on practical bee-keeping, for which excellent works exist. His subject is the life itself, watched with a poet's and a naturalist's eye.

The contents run from the threshold of the hive and the swarm through the foundation of the city and the life of the bee. Young queens, the nuptial flight, the massacre of the males, and the progress of the race follow. Maeterlinck finds in the hive a mirror of order, sacrifice, and mystery, told in luminous prose.
45708-spring-notes-from-tennessee:
Spring Notes from Tennessee is a nature and travel book by Bradford Torrey, printed at Boston by Houghton Mifflin in 1896. Torrey also wrote Birds in the Bush, A Rambler's Lease and A Florida Sketch-Book. His epigraph is Stevenson's: we travelled in the print of olden wars, yet all the land was green. The essays walk the Chattanooga battlefields in spring, watching birds.

An afternoon by the river and a morning in the north woods follow. A week on Walden's Ridge is the longest stay. Some Tennessee bird notes and a list of birds close the book. Torrey reached Chattanooga on the evening of April 26 in a rattling thunder shower. Torrey's method is to idle, look and listen, on ground where armies fought and birds now sing.
45893-william-gilbert-and-terrestial-mag:
William Gilbert and Terrestrial Magnetism in the Time of Queen Elizabeth is a discourse by Silvanus Thompson. Gilbert, its subject, is named in it the father of electrical science. He was born at Colchester in 1540. Cambridge gave him his doctor's degree in medicine in 1569.

After years of travel abroad, Gilbert settled in London in 1573. He rose high in the Royal College of Physicians there. In 1599 he became the college's president, and in 1601 physician to the Queen. He attended Elizabeth in her last illness and outlived her by eight months. His great work on the magnet appeared in 1600. The discourse says that book marks an era in magnetic science. Around it Thompson traces the older history of the compass at sea. Needle, compass card, and writers on navigation all pass in review.
45921-the-mahogany-tree:
Thackeray's bacchanalian song, The Mahogany Tree, is here privately printed at New York as a Christmas souvenir for 1910. Thackeray said in a speech that he wrote it when he was younger and used to frequent jolly assemblies, and a witness remembered his radiant face while Horace Mayhew sang it. The introduction, by a member of the Titmarsh Club circle, sets the scene: friends taking their places round the convivial board at Christmas-tide.

The song itself wishes health, and love and mirth, as fits the solemn Christmas-tide, and carouses round the stem of the jolly old tree where the night-birds perch and sing. One verse turns grave, remembering evenings and kind hearts now dust. Edmund Dulac's drawing of the author, made for a Titmarsh Club dinner menu, fronts the little book.
49091-the-man-of-galilee:
Atticus Haygood wrote this book on Jesus, the Man of Galilee. Hunt and Eaton printed it in New York in 1889. Haygood gives the book to his Emory boys of 1876 to 1884. A preface letter to Professor Lundy Harris tells its origin plainly.

Students at old Emory often asked him to fix his lecture thoughts. He wrote with the boys faces before him in Seney Hall. Contents ask if the evangelists invented Jesus at the start. No dramatist can draw taller men than himself, chapter two argues. Jesus and myths and Jesus and Hebrew human nature fill the chapters that follow next.
49195-viscount-dundee:
Viscount Dundee, by Louis Barbe, forms part of the Famous Scots series. Oliphant, Anderson and Ferrier published it at Edinburgh and London. Barbe gives the book to his sons, Louis and Adrien. Chapter one treats Dundee's family, birth, and early life. Chapter two sets out the Covenant and the Covenanters. Dispersing the conventiclers fills chapter three. Rejected addresses and civil, military, and marriage matters follow.

Chapter six is called The Killing Time. The life traces a soldier caught in Scotland's war of faith and crown. The series list at the front shows its scope, from Knox and Burns to Hume and Livingstone. Barbe writes for general readers who want a clear life in short compass. Dundee's fame rests on loyalty, force, and a hard age.
49372-ninety-three:
Victor Hugo's Ninety-Three, translated by Mrs Aline Delano, was published at Boston in 1889 among his romances. A contents map shows the design in three parts: At Sea, At Paris, In the Vendée. Part one opens in the forest of La Saudraie.

The corvette Claymore follows, with chapters named England and France United, Tormentum Belli, and He Who Sets Sail Invests in a Lottery. Halmalo and Tellmarch complete the sea part, ending No Mercy, No Quarter. Part two turns to Paris: Cimourdain, the pot-house of the Rue du Paon, and the Convention, with Marat in the green-room. Readers get Hugo's last novel, the Revolution and the royalist rising locked in one tragic year.
49379-shiloh-national-military-park-tenn:
Albert Dillahunty wrote this National Park Service historical handbook on Shiloh, number ten in the series, printed at Washington in 1955 and sold for twenty-five cents. It preserves the scene of the first great battle in the West.

The handbook recounts the two-day battle of April 6 and 7, 1862, in which nearly 24,000 men were killed, wounded, or missing. The Confederate failure there, it argues, foreshadowed the loss of the Memphis and Charleston Railroad and opened the way toward Vicksburg. A guide to the area follows: state monuments, Ruggles' batteries, the Hornets' Nest, Bloody Pond, and Pittsburg Landing. A closing section notes how Shiloh inspired writers. Visitors get battle and battlefield in one small book.
49450-petrarch-s-secret-or-the-soul-s-co:
Petrarch's Secret holds three dialogues between Petrarch and St Augustine on the soul's conflict with passion. William H Draper turned the Latin text into English. The book came out in London in 1911.

In his preface Petrarch tells how a bright lady appeared to him as he mused. He was wide awake, he says, and full of wonder at her light. The talks that follow weigh fame, love and the pull of the world. Augustine presses hard, and Petrarch speaks for his own weak heart. The work is a frank self trial by a great poet. Two plates, one of Petrarch himself, face the text.
50448-the-coronado-expedition-1540-1542-:
The Coronado Expedition, 1540 to 1542, by George Parker Winship, was excerpted from the Fourteenth Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology. Winship prepared the translation and study of the Spanish records at Washington. The expedition of Francisco Vásquez de Coronado was the first great European march into the American south west. Its reports shaped maps for three hundred years.

The contents first give the causes of the expedition: the wanderings of Cabeza de Vaca, the report of Friar Marcos de Niza, and the wealth ascribed to the Seven Cities of Cibola. The march follows: Zuñi taken, the Grand Canyon found by Cárdenas, winter at Tiguex on the Rio Grande, and the plains of buffalo to Quivira. The full narrative of Castañeda closes the work, in translation and in the Spanish text.
50618-oxford-days-or-how-ross-got-his-de:
A Resident M A wrote Oxford Days, or How Ross Got His Degree, issued at London in 1879. A short note says the book is not shaped like Verdant Green or Tom Brown at Oxford. Its aim is to be a working guide to college life. The tale form is used to make dry facts live.

Ten chapters trace Frank Ross from his first term to his gown at last. Ross was eighteen and the eldest of six brothers when the tale starts. His father and the Vicar of Porchester weigh which college to choose. Oxford was picked for school and home ties. Chapters treat a freshman term, the Eights, a long break, and a reading party. The close shows the grind and the prize.
51822-arcturus-times-three:
Jack Sharkey wrote Arcturus Times Three, a science fiction tale printed in Galaxy Magazine in October nineteen sixty-one. The hero, Jerry Norcriss, is said to have lived hundreds of lives across the Galaxy. The tale opens with a text on zoology in the year twenty ninety-seven.

Trial and error with new life forms, the text warns, is too risky on far worlds. A five-man crew can ill afford to lose one man. The tale recalls the second Mars landing, where cute beasts called quilties won the crew's hearts. Their fur hid spines, and their biology proved more like that of hornets.
52292-report-of-the-committee-of-fifteen:
The Report of the Committee of Fifteen, by Harris, Draper, and Tarbell, was read at the Cleveland meeting of the Department of Superintendence. The meeting ran February 19 to 21, 1895, and the debate that followed is printed with the report. The New England Publishing Company of Boston issued it that year. Each member kept the right to state his own points of difference at his signature.

Harris opens with the committee's agreed ground: the correlation of studies in elementary schools. First, topics must stand in logical order, each step timed to help the next, in its own branch and in kindred ones. Second, the course as a whole must mirror the great divisions of human learning, with no division left out and none crowding the rest. Third, the choice must fit the mind's own growth.
52995-spaceman-on-a-spree:
Spaceman on a Spree, a science fiction story by Mack Reynolds, ran in Worlds of Tomorrow in June 1963, with pictures by Nodel. Its hero is Space Pilot Seymour Pond, called Si, who is retiring from the Department of Space Exploration. The department gives him a gold watch, wound by the bearer's own motion, and a banquet with speeches.

Si would rather have had shares of Variable Basic to add to his savings. He has counted the cost of more trips against the space cafard, the madness brewed from shut-in fear, dullness, boredom, and free fall. A one room flat with an autochair, an autobar, and a wall screen is all the contentment he asks. The story asks what matters more, man's reach into space or one spaceman's life, and answers through a small, dry retirement.
54068-hearts-of-three:
Jack London wrote Hearts of Three, a tale of quest and daring in the Latin lands of the New World. A pirate song by George Sterling heads the book, with a chorus of rovers back to back against the mainmast. The hero is Francis Morgan, a rich young man in a fine house. His father had run vast affairs from the library where Francis now takes a late breakfast.

Events move fast for Francis that spring morning, though he does not know it yet. His valet Parker tells how the old man kept lean by half an hour of exercise in bed each day. London, known for The Valley of the Moon and his dog tales, sends his hero from ease into raw drama. Blood, plunder, and lost kin wait on the seas ahead.
57910-running-free:
James Connolly wrote Running Free, a set of sea stories printed at New York in 1917. The tales had first run in magazines between 1912 and 1917. A front plate shows a bridal couple holding hands over the spanker boom at the full moon.

Ten stories fill the book: The Strategists, The Weeping Annie, The Bull-Fight, and A Bale of Blankets lead. Breath o' Dawn, The Medicine Ship, and One Wireless Night follow. The first tale opens at Santacruz, where a lady arrives with children to join her husband of an American warship. A smiling stranger smoking under the portales, Carmen Whiffle, is marked at once as an enemy.
58155-the-bar-20-three:
Bar Twenty Three is a western novel by Clarence Mulford of Hopalong fame. Burt of New York issued it by arrangement with McClurg in nineteen twenty one. Frank Schoonover drew the frontispiece for this Bar Twenty ranch tale. Mulford also wrote Johnny Nelson, Bar Twenty Days, and Buck Peters Ranchman.

Chapter heads run from Put a T in It to well known strangers first. A question of identity, what the storm hid, and writing on the wall follow. The third man, notes compared, and ways of serving notice build the plot. The staked plain, a vigil rewarded, and a well planned raid fill later pages. The Bar Twenty three are Hopalong Cassidy and his two partners in arms.
58665-the-parthenon-at-athens-greece-and:
The Parthenon at Athens, Greece and at Nashville, Tennessee gathers excerpts from a larger work on the Parthenon of Pericles. Benjamin Wilson, director of the Parthenon at Nashville, made the book. Parthenon Press of Nashville issued it, with copyright in 1941. The dedication names the board of park commissioners of two decades.

Athens raised the first Parthenon for Athena in the age of Pericles. Nashville raised a full scale copy in plaster, then in stone, for her centennial. Wilson tells how the copy was built and what it holds. Photographs set the two temples side by side for the reader. The excerpts argue that the copy teaches the original to Americans. Few cities in the world keep a Greek temple in a park.
59643-family-tree:
Family Tree is a science fiction story by Charles L Fontenay, taken from Worlds of If for December 1956. A blurb asks if man ancestors were monkeys after all. Fontenay opens with a plain question, how do you get rid of a superman.

Masefield Truggles came to Marston Hill just two years back, while Blan Forsythe was born there and lived there all his life. Word, half in jest and half in earnest, said Forsythe had more than one wife. Truggles took reform or removal of Forsythe as his gift to the town morals. He scouted for weak spots in the man name, then began with the ex wife, Phyllis Allison, and her young son. Readers get small town spite aimed at a man who may be more than human.
59994-the-bojabi-tree:
The Bojabi Tree, by Edith Rickert, was copyrighted in 1923 and published at Garden City, New York, with pictures by Gleb Botkin. Chapter one is Robin Rat. In the land of All the Beasts, the text says, there was a great hunger.

Some of the hungry animals are named: Tabby Tiger, Bruno Bear, Katy Crocodile, Robin Rat, Pinky Pig, Giddy Goat, and Tommy Tortoise. They ran around the wood eating roots, twigs, and scraps. But still they were hungry. One day they came to a big tree full of fruit. But they could not eat it, for they did not know what it was. They sat in a circle round the tree. Let us send Robin Rat, one says. Readers get a simple beast fable for young children.
6120-soldiers-three:
Rudyard Kipling gathers Soldiers Three with The Story of the Gadsbys and In Black and White. It opens on Mulvaney's maxim: hit a man and help a woman, and you can't be far wrong anyways. The Inexpressibles give a ball, borrowing a seven-pounder from the Gunners, wreathing it with laurels, and laying a plate-glass dancing floor.

Private Mulvaney stands sentry at the door, holding trays of programme cards, while supper like none eaten before waits inside. Tales of Learoyd, the big drunk draft, the wreck of the Visigoth, and the solid Muldoon follow. Kipling writes barrack-room India with swagger, humor, and soldier talk.
61673-partners-three:
Partners Three is a boys' sea novel by Ralph Henry Barbour, illustrated by Relyea and published in Chicago by Donohue in 1913. Its hero is Jack Herrick, skipper of the launch Crystal Spring, shown nosing her way out of Herrick's Cove in the frontispiece.

The contents map a summer of salt water. A rescue makes the partnership, and a pair of amateur salts join the skipper. Buried treasure starts the plot: Bee composes an ode to the sea, plans an expedition, and digs on Nobody's Island. A man with a glass eye, a sunken wreck, and a marooning follow. Trained clams, a schooner ashore, and a gale fought by the life-boat raise the stakes. A letter in a dory and treasure trove close the hunt. Barbour wrote dozens of such tales, in which boys, boats, and buried gold keep school holidays at sea.
62295-mary-lee:
Geoffrey Dennis published the novel Mary Lee in New York in 1922. Mary tells her own story, and the first chapter states her terms at once: she was born at Tawborough on March 2, 1848. That year, she notes, fires of revolution swept Europe while her small English town slept through all of it.

Forty-five chapters in two parts follow her life. Childhood chapters bring Bear Lawn, meeting, school, an uncle named Simeon, and the end of the world as the town fears it. Mary grows curious, says goodbye, and crosses to France, where a chateau, Paris, and a sudden inheritance change her place in the world. Chapter titles keep returning to deathbeds and visions, and to the stranger who crosses her path more than once. Readers get a long, witty life story in the voice of a woman who watches her century with sharp eyes.
62682-the-old-oak-tree:
Moncrieff wrote a small picture tale for children about an old oak tree. The book was sold by Dean and Son of London as a sixpenny book. It could be had on cloth that would not tear for a shilling. Bright color plates fill its few pages. The tale starts, as tales do, with once upon a time.

The oak stands in a gent's park by a river's side. Its long arms, thick with ivy, bid all to its shade. Bunny the Rabbit dwells at its foot with his wife. Their brood counts sixteen young ones in the hole. More beasts take up homes in bough and root. Small children get a kind first tale.
64309-gama-is-thee:
Stanley Mullen sends readers to a famed animal house on Venus in a tale from Planet Stories for July 1953. A head note warns that a knock at a locked gate at night on Venus starts an adventure. Maid, monster, or both may answer the summons, the note adds with a wink.

Khaljean's — zoo, pet shop, and wild animal supply house — draws talk on Mars, Titan, Rhea, and Pluto alike, Mullen writes. Tales claim Khaljean can build a monster to order from spare parts, a claim Mullen calls a tall tale. He loves beasts and keeps ten for each one he sells, and he has risked death rather than harm a living thing. No one knows his race or source, and no one asks now.
64332-from-seven-to-seventy-memories-of-:
From Seven to Seventy: Memories of a Painter and a Yankee, by Edward Simmons, was published by Harper and Brothers in 1922, with an interruption by Oliver Herford. Herford jokes that so noted a painter needs no introduction. The title states the span: a life told from age seven to age seventy.

Chapters move from a Concord, Massachusetts childhood and Harvard College to the search for a career out west. Paris student days follow, then Brittany and Spain, St. Ives and London, and summers at Barbizon and Grez. Later chapters treat his first decorations, Stanford White, the Players, American humor, and paint and painters. Plates show the Old Manse at Concord and the author at seven and at seventy. The book is an artist's own record of the American art world he helped to build.
64532-the-lore-of-the-honey-bee:
The Lore of the Honey-Bee, by Tickner Edwardes, author of The Bee-Master of Warrilow, was first published in August 1908 by Methuen of London. It reached a third edition in 1909. Twenty-four illustrations accompany the text. Edwardes dedicates the book to Thomas William Cowan, chairman of the British Bee-Keepers' Association, to whose labours all bee-keepers owe a lasting obligation.

An introduction calls bee-keeping the oldest craft under the sun. Chapters follow the bee through history: the ancients and the honey-bee, the isle of honey, and bee-masters in the Middle Ages. The commonwealth of the hive, the genesis of the queen, and the sovereign worker-bee come next. Later chapters treat the mystery of the swarm, the comb-builders, and the drone and his story. The modern bee-farm and bee-keeping and the simple life close the volume.
65113-the-vengeance-of-toffee:
The Vengeance of Toffee is a science fiction story by Charles F Myers, printed in Imagination in February 1951. The world of the tale stands on the brink of atomic war. Bombs tick behind locked and guarded doors in remote places. Nothing, it seems, can prevent the end.

The ticking grows louder through newspapers, radios, and men's own heartbeats. A bomb, H bomb, X bomb: each new letter shortens the fuse. A broadcaster recalls the pleasant voice that once made him popular, now announcing a new kind of totalitarian death. Against this stands Toffee, with a plan and a little magic to boot. Myers mixes fantasy with the newest fears of the cold war. The story's charm is its wager that whimsy might outwit the bomb.
65931-no-time-for-toffee:
Charles F Myers wrote a comic tale first printed in Imagination in July 1952. Marc Pillsworth steps to a microphone as a scarred man lifts a gun. Glass breaks, pain blooms in his chest, and the world fades in flame. A note at the front warns that Toffee is loving him to death.

Marc wakes toward a court of great Heads who rule in Limbo mists. The Heads have grown huge brains and small bodies in chase of pure thought. They groan over Marc's death and what it means for their plans. Myers mixes pulp thrills with sly sport at ghosts, love, and fate.
66014-the-laughter-of-toffee:
The Laughter of Toffee is a science fiction story by Charles Myers. It appeared in Imagination in October 1954. A headnote sketches the hero's troubles. A miracle elixir starts them. Then come a bevy of cops, a woman called Toffee, and X-ray eyes.

Marc Pillsworth opens the tale on a spring morning. He heads for another orderly day at his advertising agency. Spring has made the whole city pleasantly silly. Marc alone feels sour and unwell. He loathes the season with all his heart. He loathes one man still more. Mario Matalini is an Italian portrait artist. Mario has taken Marc's wife Julie to the country to paint her. Jealousy is a new and gassy sensation for Marc.
66148-the-wizard-of-wall-street-and-his-:
Trumbull White wrote The Wizard of Wall Street and His Wealth, or The Life and Deeds of Jay Gould, issued at Philadelphia in 1893. The front note calls Gould the man who had won the most wealth of any man in his life. White says the tale holds much for the plain reader and for the student of finance.

Gould won his wealth by bold feats that stunned the world. His life was full of sharp turns and loud fame. White pledges full care for facts and use of all sound sources. He says the time is ripe, as all seek news of Gould. The book shows both what to copy and what to shun in Gould's path.
6650-immensee:
Theodor Storm's Immensee, in a translation by C. W. Bell, opens with a preface on a new era of understanding between nations. Language study will matter more and more, the preface says. Readers who wish to know their neighbors' speech will welcome this text. It can be read in spare moments, without a bulky dictionary. The book was made for that quiet, steady study.

Storm's tale itself is a tender German novella of youth, love, and memory, told in prose that lingers like a lake at dusk. Bell's English keeps the mood plain and lyrical. Immensee is a short, moving classic, well suited to readers meeting German literature for the first time.
6685-story-hour-readers-book-three:
Ida Coe and Alice Christie, teachers in New York public schools, made this third-year reader for young children. Its contents mix Stevenson and Longfellow with Hansel and Gretel, Cinderella, Greek myths, and Indian folklore. The Land of Story Books, The Eagle and the Fox, Hiawatha's Brothers, and The Bag of Winds all appear.

Each piece is short, clear, and made to be read aloud in class or at home. Pictures and simple type aid the young reader's first steps into great tales. Story Hour Readers, Book Three, is a warm, old-style school book, full of the stories that shaped many childhoods.
67105-the-animals-christmas-tree:
The Animals Christmas Tree is a small fable by the Reverend John P Peters, printed in New York by Dutton in 1916. It first ran in The Churchman magazine. The house says the tale was asked for so often that a book form was due.

A note adds that since the outbreak of the War, the tale truth has grown plain and weighty. Once, the fable says, the animals chose to hold a Christmas tree of their own. Swifts and swallows in country house chimneys had woke to joy and laughter and peeped in. They saw an evergreen tree hung with bright balls and threads of gold and silver, and a Christ Child or angel high in the branches. Word spread through the animal world. Young readers get a gentle beast fable with a war time moral.
67111-the-sacred-tree:
Arthur Waley turned Lady Murasaki's Tale of Genji into English in this second part of his famous version. Houghton Mifflin printed The Sacred Tree at Boston and New York in 1926, from British sheets. A list of the chief persons and family tables opens the book.

Fiction in Japan before the tale gets a long first essay, then the art of Murasaki herself. A summary of volume one sets the stage. The Sacred Tree, chapter ten of the tale, opens the story here. The Village of Falling Flowers and Exile at Suma follow, among the most loved parts of the whole. Akashi, the flood gauge, and the palace in the tangled woods fill the middle. Waley's Genji made Japan's great classic an English classic too.
67600-how-to-trace-a-pedigree:
How to Trace a Pedigree, by H A Crofton, was published in London in nineteen eleven by Elliot Stock of Paternoster Row. Crofton's guide stands among the publisher's practical handbooks for genealogists and book-lovers. Companion volumes taught readers to decipher old documents, form libraries, and make indexes.

The front advertisements sketch the world the beginner enters. A key to the family deed-chest promises help with ancient handwriting and obsolete words. Whitmore's Ancestral Tablets offer diagrams for recording eight generations of ancestors. Crofton's own text, following its title page, directs the search through records and registers. Genealogy was becoming a middle-class pursuit in Edwardian England. Such manuals turned an antiquarian hobby into a method anyone could follow at the parish chest.
67652-bring-the-jubilee:
Ward Moore wrote Bring the Jubilee, an original novel issued at New York by Farrar, Straus and Young at two dollars. Moore had writ Breathe the Air Again and Greener Than You Think. The book is given to Tony Boucher and Mick McComas, who liked the story. Quotes from Troilus and Cressida and from James Jeans head the work.

Jeans holds that the puzzle of time brings thought to a standstill. If time's true nature is forever beyond reach, so is a verdict on fate and free will, he says. Chapter One is named Life in the Twenty Six States. Decisions, minibiles, and tinugraphs fill Chapter Two in coined terms of a changed world. A member of the Grand Army and a figure named Tyss follow. The tale is an alternate history of a South that won, told from a later age.
67822-the-ghost-of-one-man-coulee:
Bower wrote this western tale, first printed in The Popular Magazine on January 1, 1913. Bower had written the Happy Family stories and Lonesome Land. A headnote tells the core of it: Olafson the violinist went out in a blizzard, lost seeking the north wind that he might learn the song it sang. Happy Jack holds that Olafson comes back on moonlight nights to play his violin in the doorway of the deserted shack in One Man Coulee.

Happy Jack tells the tale to the Native Son, Miguel, whose silver spurs jingle beside his heel. The old fiddler, Happy says, went crazy trying to play a tune like the wind, and killed himself because he could not make it stick. Miguel answers with a cool smile. Some moonlight night, he says, the two of them will come back at midnight and listen, for he is fond of music.
68016-the-girl-avenger-or-the-beautiful-:
The Girl Avenger, or the beautiful terror of the Maumee, is a pocket novel by Captain Charles Howard, issued by a New York dime novel house. Its copyright was entered in 1872. Howard's other pocket novels are listed by number on the title page, with names like The Wolf Queen and The Mad Chief. The first chapter is called Stricken over the Dead.

It was evening, the tale opens, among the tall cottonwoods and poplars along the Maumee river. The dying day was an August one in the year 1794. A stag came to the historic stream to drink, its antlered head held high. Yet its careful tread showed that it sensed hidden foes close by. Its eyes swept the wood on left and right, and the far bank as well.
68417-the-lighting-of-the-christmas-tree:
The Lighting of the Christmas Tree is a short play in the Vassar Series of Plays. Josephine Palmer and Annie Thorp adapted it from The Christmas Guest, a story by Selma Lagerlöf. Samuel French published it in New York, with copyrights of 1917 and 1921. Amateurs could act it on payment of a five-dollar royalty for each performance.

The play brings Lagerlöf's Christmas tale to the school and parlour stage. Its series, edited by Gertrude Buck, supplied colleges with short plays of literary quality. The Christmas tree lighting of the title forms the heart of the piece. The acting edition gives the full text with the publisher's terms printed at the front.
68715-woman-free:
Woman Free is a poem by Ellis Ethelmer, issued in eighteen ninety three. A women's emancipation union published it, at five shillings post free. A French quotation with its English rendering heads the verse. The philosopher, studying the laws of nature, grows sure that all evils spring from their abuse alone, it says. The poem opens with the source of light that cheers this later day.

Science calm moves to spread her sovereign sway, the verse begins. Research and reason stand ranged on either hand of her, it says. Man may see amendment for his previous rule from every stage of slow degree, the poem argues. His keener conscience in our fuller time perceives the once careless act a crime. The sense of freedom as a strong instinct in all creatures is weighed later.
68904-one-of-three:
One of Three is a tale of the far worlds by Wesley Long, first put out in a pulp sheet of such tales in the third month of nineteen forty eight. Its first part bears a one word head: touch. A bit of white stuff in a test tube glows in the beam, which is its wont. It shakes as well, most soft, which is not its wont at all.

That shake had not been known past this hour. But the stuff was made of false forms of the fire ore from the great piles. All too small a store of lore is held on such things. The fact that this one shook, each time the beam struck it, held the eye of both the man of lore and the mere keen man.
69431-thomas-d-arcy-mcgee:
Alexander Brady's Thomas D'Arcy McGee, from the Macmillan Company of Canada at Toronto in 1925, tells the life of Canada's most eloquent champion of Confederation. Brady, a lecturer in political science at the University of Toronto, thanks the Toronto Reference Library and Doughty of the Dominion Archives. He thanks too the subject's brother McGee of Ottawa for the family material.

The chapters run Youth, The Lessons of Experience, The Prophet of Canadian Nationality, In Office and Out of It, Confederation and Fenianism, and Closing Years. McGee reached Montreal in 1857 at thirty-two, already a poet, a journalist of five newspapers, and a fugitive rebel of a lost Irish cause. Within months he sat in the colonial legislature; within ten years his public life was crushed into triumph and cut short by a bullet.
70255-fancy-free:
Fancy Free is a book of tales by Eden Phillpotts, published by Methuen in London in 1901. Eight illustrations by several hands accompany the stories. Phillpotts dedicates the volume to Francis Cowley Burnand with hearty regard. His earlier novels, Children of the Mist among them, stand listed at the front.

The Zagabog opens the collection in bouncing comic verse. Its hero rules a golden island beyond the sun in that rhyme. He wears an ugly crown, has green and somewhat sad eyes, and sits on early mud. Quite out of the common, Johnson's Boswell, and the nine musketeers follow. The mate of a ship and the transmigrations of Tarver come later. A celestial chat and an archdeacon among dinosaurs close the fantastical set.
70498-the-evergreen-tree:
Evergreen Tree is a Christmas masque by Percy MacKaye, the civic dramatist. Appleton of New York issued the masque among his community dramas list. MacKaye also wrote Caliban, a community masque, and Sanctuary, a bird masque. The Canterbury Pilgrims and Jeanne D Arc stand among his earlier plays.

A dance carol of the evergreen is pictured in the front matter here. Sing our even song and dance for thee, O evergreen, it runs. King and queen in the dance vow to make the tree heart merry. MacKaye civic theatre essays argue drama as a public rite for towns. This short masque gives a town a Christmas rite in verse and dance.
70761-destiny-times-three:
Fritz Leiber wrote a science fiction tale that first ran in Astounding Science Fiction in March and April 1945. The tale opens with a color concert retelling the old Norse myth of Yggdrasil, the great tree of life. Thorn, one of the men watching, sees the myth match a bold claim he and Clawly plan to put before the World Executive Committee.

Their claim holds that more than one stream of time runs side by side, and that dark forces gnaw at those roots like the serpents in the myth. A hooded stranger, impossibly old, joins Clawly in urgent whispers as the concert ends. Thorn then feels a blind force from beyond the stars seize his hand and use him as its tool. Readers who like time tales with a mythic frame will find a tense, strange opening here.
71099-maggie-lee:
Maggie Lee is a volume of tales by Mary Holmes, issued at Toronto in 1881. Ross Robertson cheap series offered popular reading at popular prices to buyers. Contents list Bad Spelling, Diamonds, Maggie Lee, and The Answered Prayer as the four pieces. Holmes had won her public with Lena Rivers, Tempest and Sunshine, and Meadow Brook.

Bad Spelling opens at Madame Duvant fashionable seminary on the first day of term. The head mistress scans young faces and reckons the gain from each pupil in silence. A low hum and suppressed titters fill the schoolroom of the fashionable girls. Holmes domestic sentiment drives the tales of school, love, and answered prayer.
71482-cringle-and-cross-tree:
