Oliver Optic wrote Cringle and Cross-Tree, a sea tale put out at Boston in 1873. Rights were held from 1871 by William T Adams, the true name of the writer. The book is the fourth in a set called Upward and Onward. Fourteen plates fill the tale.

Phil Farringford, hero of the set, goes to sea in this book. His past time on a yacht on Lake Michigan had readied him in part. The first word says he fits his new life with speed and with grit. His mates in the front of the ship fall below the mean mark of men at sea. Phil holds fast to his faith and wins sway over some of them. Vice pays heed to worth, the writer claims, and reform can grow in foul air. A trip to the coast of Africa gives the tale its seas and its risks.
71567-a-new-graft-on-the-family-tree:
Pansy, whose true name was Isabella Alden, wrote a tale of faith and home life printed in London in 1902. Alden wrote many such tales, among them A Hedge Fence and Side by Side. Her new book asks in its first chapter if a new graft on a family tree will bloom or wither.

A girl of sixteen opens the tale with a sharp question about a pile of tidies. From there the story follows a household as new folk, new work, and a new Sabbath class enter its life. Chapters named New Light, Grace Sufficient, and First Fruits show a slow change of heart. Storm, doubt, and full surrender mark the path to the close.
71664-noel-s-christmas-tree:
Amy Le Feuvre's story for children opens in a schoolroom at the top of a London house in Kensington. Diana, thin, pale, and wiry, lies by the fire writing a story and sucking her pencil. Her brother Chris drums on the windowpane. A taxi has arrived below with much luggage, and the children are forbidden the hall. An unknown mother and an unknown brother are coming home from India.

Chris swears he saw a monkey, a parrot, and a huge bunch of coco-nuts. Then a shrill voice in the hall announces new boots with buttons, and the children know brother Noel by sound. The contents promise Wistaria Cottage, the Christmas tree, a nursery entertainment, and a girl named Inez who makes a vow. Later chapters speak of life without a mother, and of a journey to the borderland and back. The glory of the tree ends the book.
71973-the-shades-of-toffee:
Charles Myers wrote a wild tale called The Shades of Toffee, first run in Fantastic Adventures in June 1950. Marc Pillsworth is a young dabbler who holds that some laws of nature are vain and should be struck off the books, gravity among them. In his basement lab he pours a green liquid with great care, to the last drop.

The vat blows up in a scream of light and tears a hole in the wall, and night rushes in. Marc is hurled up, then plunged down and down into black depths, with fear coiling in his gut like a snake. He lands in a strange place with no clear cause or aim. The head note says the stuff he made was ruin, plots, and madness in a vial.
72415-the-spirit-of-toffee:
Charles Myers tells a wild ghost tale in The Spirit of Toffee, first printed in Fantastic Adventures in November 1948. Marc Pillsworth runs an ad firm and has cash and home woes of his own. His plight turns worse when a shoe hangs in mid-air in his office. The shoe marks the return of George, a ghost who is Marc in form but not in soul. Where Marc is grave, fair, and shy, George is brash, sly, and fond of show.

George first came when he wrongly thought Marc had died by his own hand. Since then the ghost has made mayhem to push that death to pass, so his own place as a haunt would be safe. Myers plays the clash for laughs and chills at once. The tale pits a staid boss against his own wild twin.
72532-hardtack-and-coffee:
John Billings served with the Army of the Potomac, in Sickles' Third and Hancock's Second Corps, and in 1887 he published Hardtack and Coffee, the unwritten story of army life. Charles Reed, of the Ninth Massachusetts Battery, drew over two hundred sketches and six color plates for it.

The chapters take up what the battle histories skip: enlisting, life in tents and log huts, jonahs and beats, offences and punishments. Raw recruits, foraging, corps badges, the wagon trains, and the army mule follow. Billings wrote the soldier's day, his food, his jokes, and his grievances, and veterans recognized themselves. The book became the classic account of the Union common soldier, still quoted wherever the Civil War is studied closely.
72669-the-mis-rule-of-three:
Florence Warden, who wrote The House on the Marsh, built this tale of three men and one girl. Unwin printed The Mis-Rule of Three in London in 1904. Its chapter heads play the theme straight: they discuss the girl; they find the girl.

Somebody's ideal and somebody's aversion come next — and was it aversion, the list asks. A bolt from the blue, somebody's luggage, and a mystery or a crime build the tangle. Rivals, a secret for sale, and the blackmailers turn the plot dark. The diggings of the three men sit off Tottenham Court Road, in a tall old house past its best days. Its last head gives the end away in form: the rule of three becomes the rule of one.
73091-the-taking-of-cloudy-mcgee:
W C Tuttle wrote a western tale of the town of Lost Hills. Its first man is Ferdinand Putney, the town's one lawyer. Putney stands six feet three, weighs little for his height, and wears a green tinged derby. He has studied law, the tale adds, a little.

The second man is Amos Weed, cashier of the town bank. Amos spends his days over columns of figures. For years he has dreamed of being a great wrong doer, a master mind. Each plan ends in a dream of the rope, and he drops it. One day he shuts the bank early and slips to the lawyer's office. Tuttle wrote many such tales of small western towns and their sly folk.
7335-jack-harkaway-and-his-son-s-escape-:
Bracebridge Hemyng's Jack Harkaway and His Son's Escape from the Brigands of Greece continues Jack Harkaway and His Son's Adventures in Greece. Its first chapter opens with the contessa's letter to Mr Mole, pleasure bent, a mendicant friar, midnight marauders, and house breaking. Mrs Harkaway's maid, scolded for a long errand, answers with twenty excuses, none of them true.

The frontispiece shows Mr Mole crying bother the beggars, and the tone stays that of a boys' adventure serial: villains, disguises, and narrow escapes in Greek hills. Hemyng writes for readers who want the next thrill at once, and this volume supplies it. Jack and his son face brigands with pluck and good humour.
73516-the-marchioness-of-brinvilliers-th:
Albert Smith turned the most famous poisoning case of old France into a romance of old Paris. Bentley published it at London in 1886, with illustrations worked from John Leech's etchings. The Marchioness of Brinvilliers and her lover Sainte-Croix stand at the center. Around them move the apothecary Glazer and his man Panurge, the poison-dealer Exili, and Louise Gauthier, who falls into the hands of the valet Lachaussee.

The contents run through the catacombs of the Bievre, the Bastille, and Versailles. The mischief thickens through orgies at the Hotel de Cluny and a flight to Liege. At the end come the trap, the examination of the Marchioness, the water question, and the Place de Greve. Smith, a showman as much as a novelist, plays the Affair of the Poisons for melodrama, and the seventeenth century supplies him real horrors enough.
73944-the-green-bay-tree:
Louis Bromfield published The Green Bay Tree with Stokes in 1924, his first novel. Grosset and Dunlap reprinted it for the cheap shelves. He dedicates it to his mother, who must have known, at some time in her life, a Hattie Tolliver.

The dedication letter states the novel's theme. Life is hard for our children, it says. Their grandfathers were pioneers, and the same blood runs in their veins. Only they have no frontier any longer. They stand with their backs to the rough-hewn Middle West and their faces toward Europe and the East. They belong to neither, and are lost somewhere between. Bromfield sets his industrial Ohio family against that loss. The book made his name, and the green bay tree of the psalm stands over a town that mills are swallowing.
74787-the-happy-tree:
The Happy Tree is a novel by Murray, author of past books of the years just past. It came out at London in the mid nineteen twenties, printed in Britain, with all rights kept. A Greek tag heads the book, with its English turn by Pope set below.

Like leaves on trees the race of man is found, those lines run. Green now in youth, now sere on the ground. A new race the next spring gives, as they fall in turn and rise in turn. So the breeds of men wane in their course, and so these thrive when those are past. The tale then opens its first part, named Green Felicity, as leaves fall from a tree at a gate.
75609-the-aldine-speller-part-three:
Catherine Bryce of Minneapolis and Frank Sherman, once a school head in Monson, Massachusetts, made this spelling book for grades five and six. Newson and Company copyrighted it in 1916 as part three of the Aldine Speller. The opening pages speak first to teachers, not pupils.

Oral spelling, the authors say, should come before written work in the early grades. Clear speech must come first too, since a child cannot spell a word well that he cannot say well. Long words are broken into parts when first shown, with a slight pause between them, though in writing they must stay whole and undivided.
76849-this-star-shall-be-free:
This Star Shall Be Free is a science fiction story by Murray Leinster. Its headnote says that Tork, a simple man of the caves, could not dream what power the star box held. It might make his people gods, or hold only a lost memory in stone. The tale is set in a far past England and France.

Cave folk live in chalk cliffs above a river, in the tale's telling. An urge to move east comes on them, which they cannot explain. It is part of an experiment by beings from Antares, though the cave folk cannot guess that. A ship from Antares had passed two hours before the urge came. Tork, a young hunter, spears fish from a rock when the ship goes over. One Ear, the boss male of the colony, rules the caves with his fists.
77219-kitty-s-christmas-tree:
Lucy Ellen Guernsey wrote this Sunday school tale, issued at Philadelphia by the American Sunday-School Union under copyright in 1869. It stands as a prequel to her tale The Heiress of McGregor. Kitty Tremain comes home late from school one October day, her face swollen with crying, while her mother watches at the door.

Kitty's fault, her cousin Tilly says, is that she can be coaxed into anything, just like her father. Her mother hopes she is gaining firmness, and the tale tests that hope. The subtitle names the danger: the net of the flatterer, spread in vain only for the bird that sees it. Six short chapters carry a plain moral for young girls, in the earnest manner of its day.
77324-the-dark-year-of-dundee:
The Dark Year of Dundee is a tale of the Scottish Reformation, published by Nelson in London and Edinburgh in 1867. The author, unnamed on the title page, had written other tales of martyr times. The story opens in the early summer of 1544. A dark cloud looms over every home in Dundee, and the angel of the pestilence stands with sword outstretched, though no eye yet beholds him.

The contents divide the tale into trials and deliverances. Chapters named Fanaticism, Clouded Death, and God's Messenger open the book. A cardinal's missionary arrives, and the story follows how his mission sped and what became of him. Clear shining after rain closes the tale. A second story, The Prior's Tithe, fills the back of the volume. The book is Protestant historical fiction of the Victorian kind, written to keep Reformation memory warm.
77327-the-work-of-the-war-refugees-commi:
Lady Lugard gave a speech on the work of the War Refugees Committee to the Royal Society of Arts on March 24, 1915, printed in London that year. Britain had taken in crowds of Belgians driven from their homes by the German invasion. Lugard calls their flight one of the saddest chapters in the island's long past.

She grants that a sea moat and a strong navy let Britain serve as a refuge, as it had so often before. Oddly, she traces the committee's roots to Ulster plans made before the war, when civil strife in Ireland was the feared storm. Those plans to move women and children from a war zone were turned, in weeks, to a far larger task of mercy.
77471-the-loyal-mountaineers-of-tennesse:
The Loyal Mountaineers of Tennessee, by Thomas William Humes, was published at Knoxville in 1888 by Ogden Brothers. A plate shows the assault on Fort Sanders. Humes quotes Ruskin on the title page: the noblest word in the catalogue of social virtues is loyalty. The book is dedicated to the memory of two friends and helpers of a suffering people.

The preface argues that East Tennessee's stand in the Civil War of 1861 to 1865 had no precise parallel. Most of its people chose the Union and held to it, ringed by seceded states. The border slave states kept their governments loyal, Humes grants. But their ground was far less hostile than the mountains of East Tennessee. His history defends a Unionist South against the simpler story of a solid Confederacy.
77741-a-treatise-concerning-the-properti:
Benjamin Moseley, a doctor at Chelsea Hospital, wrote a treatise on coffee, here in its fifth edition at London in 1792. The first edition came out at the start of 1785, and four more were called for. Moseley adds fresh proof and the words of past writers to back his claims.

He argues that wide use of coffee would help both health and trade. More coffee grown in the British West Indian islands, he says, would bring in revenue and supply a good now close to a need of daily life. Hard times for planters, from storms and heavy taxes, make his plea more urgent.
78734-sparing-the-family-tree:
Sparing the Family Tree is a western tale by Tuttle, author of Shepherds for Science. Its narrator, Brown, opens by doubting his partner's pedigree. Taos Thompson says he didn't come from no place and ain't got no definite place to go, and down in the cactus country, Brown reflects, nobody cares what a man calls himself.

Brown met Taos in the desert, finding him trying to gather himself into the shade of a two foot snag of mesquite, just about to cash in from drouth. Offered the canteen, the sufferer grinned through split lips: if that's the best you've got. Taos proves the only prospector Brown ever knew who didn't care whether he found gold or not; he loved to prospect for its own sake. Taos, red topped, with freckled hands unmatched for drawing a big Colt, pays his way and asks favors of no man.
79142-judith-lee:
Judith Lee earns her bread teaching the deaf to read lips, and her gift runs in the blood. Her father taught the oral system; her deaf mother spoke by watching mouths. Judith can catch speech at any range her eyes can reach. Richard Marsh built these tales, out in 1912, on that one strange skill.

The first case starts with a shock: a man catches her hair and saws it from her head. Later pages bring eavesdropping at Interlaken, a bomb by a bed, and a den at Elm Grove. Marsh wrote tales of crime and the uncanny; here the detective's tool is sight, not sound.
79218-eyes-that-cannot-see:
Albert Gnudtzmann wrote Eyes That Cannot See, a play in one act, translated from the Danish by Arvid Paulson and published at Cincinnati in 1923 in the Stewart Kidd Modern Plays series. The translator dedicates the English version to the memory of Richard Mansfield, who died in the service of his country.

The cast is small: Hammelev, a public school teacher; his wife; their son Anton; Louise Thorsen; and Kirsten. The action fills the living quarters of a Danish country school, first produced at the Royal Theatre in Copenhagen on September 10, 1903. The stage shows a low-ceilinged room with antique furniture and garden windows. Readers get a Danish one-act of family blindness, built for the little-theatre stage.
79230-with-the-one-coin-for-fee:
Helen Hull wrote a short story, one of four in a book dated 1940, set in a shore town in southern New England. The town lies on a river at the head of a bay, with docks, stores, and homes that climb the hills. Strange, sweet air in the heart of a great storm hangs over the place as the tale starts.

Hull says that pent air can free the blood of habit, hate, and age for a brief spell. An old house on a point of shore, with bay on one side and river on the other, anchors the scene. A ferry crossed at night for one coin gives the tale its name and its charge.
79274-coffee:
Coffee is a trade book on the bean, its past, kinds, and traits. Joseph Walsh wrote it in 1894, fresh from a like book on tea. It came out in Philadelphia and two more towns that year. The first part takes up the early past of the drink.

Walsh says the trade in coffee had grown vast by his day. Ships, hands, and funds in great sums were tied to the bean. Yet its first years are lost in tales, not in firm facts. No sign of the plant shows in the days of the old kings of Egypt. Its home is placed up the Nile, by the tales he weighs. The book then sorts the kinds of coffee and tells their traits.
79539-squee:
Squee is a science fiction story by Margaret St Clair, with a plate by Murphy. A head note says hope for man rests on one lesson, that some things must not be done, even to win. The tale asks if men have learned it.

A crew sleeps with feet in each other faces and breathes the same air over and over. Save for Neil laboratory, they live in half dark. They never have quite enough to eat, and their water comes from their own wastes cleaned and used again. They have lived so for near three years, with a year or more to go before Earth. Jacobsen, a big clown and mimic, keeps them sane by drawing their quarrels onto himself. Space fans get a grim ship tale with a moral sting.
79736-journal-of-a-residence-in-ashantee:
Joseph Dupuis, late British envoy and consul for the kingdom of Ashantee, published his Journal of a Residence in Ashantee with Colburn in 1824. A map and plates illustrate it, including the court in audience costume, swearing fidelity to the British Government.

Dupuis travelled from Cape Coast Castle to Coomassy, the Ashanti capital. His journal records the road: Dutch forts, ruined Fantee towns, formidable serpents, and a war in progress. The book prefixes an account of the origin and causes of the present war. His researches draw chiefly on Arabic manuscripts and on information from the Moslems of Guinea. Dupuis had negotiated a treaty the government in London disowned, and the journal is his defense. It remains a primary source for the Ashanti court at its height.
9101-domestic-cookery-useful-receipts-an:
Elizabeth Ellicott Lea wrote this cookery book for young housekeepers, reaching a third edition on warm praise. Lea entered domestic duties young and felt her own ignorance keenly. She found books for elegant dishes, but few for the plain, useful work of a house. This book fills that gap, with care and good sense.

Receipts cover everyday cooking, with added hints on economy and order. Lea's motto praises wise economy as the source of liberal deeds. The book now serves as a window on the American kitchen of its day, practical, thrifty, and kind.
9595-the-conflict-with-slavery-part-1-fr:
Part one of volume seven of Whittier's works opens his prose on the conflict with slavery. Justice and Expediency leads, with The Abolitionists, their sentiments and objects, close behind. Letters to Samuel E. Sewall, John Quincy Adams, and essays on the Bible and slavery follow. What Is Slavery and Democrat and Slavery press the moral case in plain terms.

Later essays in the part treat Carlyle on the slave question, the founding of the American Anti-Slavery Society, and the lesson and duty of reformers. Whittier writes as a veteran of the cause, not a bystander. A reader gets abolitionist prose at its source, firm, clear, and steeped in the fight.
a-life-of-gen-robert-e-lee: John Esten Cooke writes a life of General Robert E. Lee. Part one follows Lee's early life, the Lees of Virginia, Light Horse Harry Lee, and Stratford. Lee's army career, resignation, and reception at Richmond follow, with the war's beginning. Cooke, a Virginia writer, tells Lee's story with Southern sympathy.
a-master-s-degree:
Margaret Hill McCarter dedicates her novel to the Kansas boys and girls who have not yet earned their degrees. The story begins at Sunrise College. Professor Vincent Burgess of Boston arrives there to teach Greek. On the same September day, Vic Burleigh enrolls as a freshman. Burleigh is a big country boy from beyond the Walnut River.

Fifteen chapters follow college games, storms, a stolen silver pitcher, and the troubles of students and teachers on the Kansas prairie. Burgess and Burleigh grow through loss, duty, and hard choices. McCarter writes a wholesome campus tale about education as character, aimed at young readers of her day.
britannica-1911-barbey-d-aurevilly-jules:
Jules Amedee Barbey dAurevilly was a French man of books who lived from eighteen eight to eighteen eighty-nine. He was born in a small town in Manche. His most famed tales came in the mid part of his life. One was struck at on its first print for a charge of foul morals.

His tales deal with a kings rising past poor farm folk, with a knight, and with wild deeds of crime. He held the most stern of old faith views yet writ on the most bold themes. He put on lord airs and hinted at a dark past. In truth his folk were plain and his youth was dull.
britannica-1911-base-fee:
Base fee, in law, is a term of English property law explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It means a freehold estate of inheritance that is limited or qualified by certain conditions, so that it can come to an end. The commonest example arises when a tenant in tail not in possession bars the entail. He acts without the consent of the protector of the settlement, the person whose agreement the law required.

Limits define that estate. Such an owner bars his own issue from succeeding. He cannot bar any remainder or reversion, the rights of others waiting behind his line, so the estate ends when his issue in tail fails. A second kind is land held by heirs general but ending on an uncertain event. An older sense meant land held by base service at the lord's will. George Eliot used a base fee in the plot of Felix Holt.
britannica-1911-bawbee:
Bawbee is the Scottish name for a halfpenny or other small coin, explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. From that use, the word widened to mean money in general. The most likely guess given is that it is a worn-down form of Sillebawby, the name of the mint master by whom the coins were first issued, about 1541. A writer of 1573, quoted in Tytler's History of Scotland, calls the bawbee worth an English penny and a quarter.

One rival tale is set aside. The word was sometimes spelled “babie,” tied by some to a “baby coin.” The entry calls that the less likely tale. In daily talk the smallest coin came to stand for cash itself.
britannica-1911-bristol-tennessee:
Bristol is a city split by a state line, lying in Sullivan county, Tennessee, and Washington county, Virginia, 130 miles north-east of Knoxville at about 1700 feet. Its people grew from 3209 in 1880 to 13,395 in 1910, with 7148 on the Tennessee side and 6247 in Virginia. Four railways make it a rail centre of some weight.

Near great mineral fields of five states, the city distributes iron, coal and coke and runs tanneries, lumber mills, iron furnaces, tobacco and furniture factories and packing houses. Sullins College for women and the Virginia Institute for Women stand on the Virginia side, a normal college for negroes on the Tennessee side. The boundary runs through the main street, dividing two separate corporations, the Virginia part having been called Goodson before its city charter in 1890.
britannica-1911-calipash-and-calipee:
Calipash and calipee are parts of the turtle used as food. This very short 1911 Britannica entry defines the two terms. Both are gelatinous substances found in the turtle's shells. The calipash comes from the upper shell. The calipee comes from the lower shell. The two differ plainly in colour. Calipash is a dull greenish shade. Calipee is a light yellow instead.

The entry links the words to carapace, the turtle's upper shell. It offers that link as a possible origin only. Nothing more is said about cooking or trade in the notice. The whole entry runs to two sentences in the original. Its content is the pair of definitions and the colours. A reader gets the meaning of the terms and little else. That is an honest measure of the text.
britannica-1911-chiemsee:
Chiemsee, also called Bayrisches Meer, is the largest lake in Bavaria, lying on a high plateau 1,600 feet above the sea. It sits between the rivers Inn, to which it drains through the Alz, and Salzach. The lake runs six miles long and nine miles broad, with an area of about 33 square miles. Three islands lie in it, Herrenwörth, Frauenwörth and Krautinsel, each named in the entry.

Herrenwörth, beautifully wooded, holds the romantic castle that Louis II of Bavaria built there, and it was a bishop's seat from 1215 to 1805. The north and south shores are flat, while hills flank the other banks and give wide views. Clear water holds trout and carp, though fishing rights are strictly kept. Steamers ply on the lake, and the Rosenheim to Salzburg railway skirts the southern shore.
britannica-1911-coffee:
Coffee is a prized foodstuff drawn chiefly from Coffea arabica, a plant of the madder family. It grows wild in Abyssinia and spread first through southern Arabia. Its name may come from an Arabic word for the drink. Some trace it instead to Kaffa, a district of Abyssinia where the tree grows wild. The genus holds about 25 kinds in the Old World tropics.

Long sections trace where the plant grows and how trade in it runs. Liberian coffee gained fame after leaf disease struck Ceylon. Sierra Leone and Congo kinds also hold trade value. Arabia sells its crop under the name Mocha. Abyssinia ships two kinds, Harrari and Habashi. The entry weighs leaf use as well, and finds it poor beside seed use. Seed demand rules the crop.
britannica-1911-committee: Committee, a word for a person or body trusted with a task, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It comes from an old French form of a Latin verb meaning to entrust. In one legal sense it names those given charge of the person or estate of a lunatic by a court. In common use it means a group chosen to deal with set business.
britannica-1911-conditional-fee:
A conditional fee, in English common law, was an estate in land tied to a set line of heirs. The gift might run to the heirs of a man's body, or to his heirs male. The name came from a condition in the gift, stated or implied. If the holder died without such heirs, the land went back to the donor.

In other words, the fee was simple in form but hung on one event. Once the holder had issue, the condition counted as met. The estate was then treated as absolute in his hands. That loose state did not last in law. The statute De Donis Conditionalibus turned the conditional fee into an estate tail. The entry points to real property for the fuller tale. Its scope is the old form, its one condition and its change by statute.
britannica-1911-cow-tree:
The cow-tree, or milk-tree, is Brosimum Galactodendron, of the natural order Moraceae. It is a native of Venezuela. Like other members of its order, it holds a milky latex in its stem. That latex flows out in large amounts when a notch is cut in the bark. Men drink the flow as it runs from the tree.

The milk is sweet and pleasant to the taste, by the entry's account. A kin species gains a note beside it. Brosimum Alicastrum, the bread-nut tree, grows in central America and Jamaica. Its fruit is cooked and eaten by the folk of those lands. The bread-fruit tree forms an allied genus of the same order. The hosted entry is short and holds no size, leaf or use past the milk. Tree, land of birth, sweet flow and two kin plants form its facts.
britannica-1911-cree:
The Cree are a tribe of North American Indians of Algonquian stock. The entry counts them at some 15,000 people, so they remain a considerable tribe. They live chiefly in Manitoba and Assiniboia. Their country lies about Lake Winnipeg and along the Saskatchewan river. Those points of place and number frame the whole short account of the tribe.

In earlier days the Cree gave trouble through constant attacks on the Sioux and the Blackfeet. The entry states that they are now peaceable and orderly. For fuller detail it sends readers to the Handbook of American Indians, published at Washington in 1907. The change from raiding to settled order is the one turn of events the entry records.
britannica-1911-decree:
Decree, from the Latin decernere, is a firm ruling that has the force of law. It is also the judgment of a court of justice. In Roman law, a decree was the ruling of the emperor on a case sent up to him. He stood as the highest judge of the realm. In church law, the term named a ruling of a church council on a point of faith in doubt.

In English law, decree meant more the judgment of a court of equity. Since the Judicature Acts, the word judgment is used for the rulings of all parts of the high court. A decree nisi is the first, open order for the end of a marriage by the divorce court. It is made final after six months if no good cause is shown against it.
britannica-1911-fee:
Fee, in law, is an estate in land held of a superior lord on condition of homage or service. In English law it means an estate of inheritance. Such an estate passes to the grantee's heirs while any exist, unlike an estate for life. It divides into three kinds: fee simple, conditional fee and fee tail. A fee farm rent is the yearly rent kept back when land in fee simple is granted.

Fee also means payment for services, above all a doctor's or lawyer's honorarium. It covers fixed sums for entering an examination or joining a society. The entry digs into the obscure roots of feudum, fief and fee. It weighs links to an old word for cattle and property, fehu. It also tests rival accounts of how the feudal term was formed.
britannica-1911-filigree:
Filigree is jewel work of a delicate kind made with twisted threads of gold and silver, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with the word itself. Older spellings ran to filigrain or filigrane. The term runs through Italian, French, Spanish, and German in like forms. The usual guess derives it from Latin words for thread and grain.

Professor Skeat gave a rival source, from a Spanish verb meaning to spin. In modern times filigree has become a special branch of jewel work. In ancient times it was part of the ordinary work of the jeweller. The entry cites a memoir of 1861 on the jewellery of the ancients. That work held that all Etruscan jewellery was of this fine wired kind.
britannica-1911-franklin-tennessee:
Franklin is a town and the county-seat of Williamson county, Tennessee, on the Harpeth river about 20 miles south-west of Nashville. Its population was 2924 in 1910. The Louisville and Nashville railway serves it, and it holds the Tennessee Female College and the Battle Ground Academy.

The town is best known for the battle fought there on 30 November 1864. General Schofield, falling back before Hood and held up at the river, entrenched south of the town and beat off repeated assaults from mid-afternoon until nine at night. He then crossed the river in good order before midnight. Confederate losses ran to about 6500 men, with six generals killed, against Union losses of 2326. The entry gives the ground, the forces, and the cost in detail.
britannica-1911-galilee:
Galilee was a Roman province of Palestine north of Samaria, bounded by the Jordan east, the Leontes north and the Mediterranean west, some 60 miles by 30. Its name means a ring or border. In Isaiah it is Galil ha-Goyim, the border of the foreigners, for Phoenicians, Syrians and Aramaeans hemmed it on three sides. The Old Testament gives it no history; the tribes of Issachar, Zebulon, Asher and Naphtali are its units.

After the exile Galilee lay with the peoples planted by the Assyrians; its reconquest is credited to John Hyrcanus. Under Rome it was a Herodian tetrarchate: Herod held it in 47 B.C., his son Antipas in 4 B.C. It was the land of Christ's boyhood and the centre of his work. After Jerusalem fell, the rabbinic schools took refuge here. Safed and Tiberias keep teachers' tombs, Maimonides among them. A ridge divides Upper from Lower Galilee.
britannica-1911-ghee:
Ghee, a kind of clarified butter made in the East, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The best sort comes from the butter of cow's milk, and a lesser sort from that of buffaloes. The butter is melted over a slow fire and left to cool. The thick pale part that rises is the ghee, and it makes up most of the butter.

A poorer kind is mixed with ground-nut oil and sold cheap. Ghee can also be made by boiling butter, skimming it, and straining it through cloth once the water is gone. In India ghee is a daily food and goes into all that Brahmans eat. It is used in rites as well, and old books on healing praise it for the eyes, the voice, and the mind.
britannica-1911-gilbert-de-la-porree:
Gilbert de la Porree (1070-1154) was a scholastic logician and theologian, born at Poitiers. The 1911 Britannica entry has him taught by Bernard of Chartres and Anselm of Laon, then teaching some twenty years at Chartres. From 1137 he lectured on logic and theology at Paris, and in 1142 he became bishop of Poitiers.

His views on the Trinity drew the church's condemnation. The synod of Reims in 1148 won papal approval for four propositions against his tenets, and his works were condemned until corrected. Gilbert submitted quietly and stayed friendly with his opponents until his death on 4 September 1154. The entry's main weight falls on his logic: his De sex principiis, on Aristotle's categories, was treated with near-Aristotelian reverence, and Dante names him master of the six principles.
britannica-1911-guarantee:
Guarantee is an old French form of the word warrant. It names a broad and weighty kind of engagement. It can mean a treaty securing rights or possessions between states. More commonly it means a private transaction. One person answers for another to win that person trust or credit. In English law it is a contract. The guarantor answers for a third person's debt or duty.

That contract is collateral to the main obligation. It does not extinguish the original liability. If the principal obligation fails, the guarantee fails with it. The surety's duties depend on the principal debtor's. The parties are named with care: surety, creditor and principal debtor. Rules from many civil codes are compared at length. France, Spain, Portugal, Italy and Egypt all figure. American usage, which separates surety from guarantor, is also examined.
britannica-1911-jeejeebhoy-sir-jamsetjee:
Sir Jamsetjee Jeejeebhoy (1783–1859) was an Indian merchant and philanthropist, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells his rise from poverty. He was born in Bombay in 1783, of poor but respectable parents. He was left an orphan early in life. At sixteen, with a smattering of trade schooling and a bare pittance, he began his travels.

Those business travels were destined to lead him to fortune and fame. After a first visit to Calcutta, he undertook a voyage to China. Such a voyage then held so much risk that it counted as a bold venture. He went on to set up a steady trade with that country. He acted as carrier of his own wares on the passages to and fro. His ships ran between Bombay, Canton, and Shanghai.
britannica-1911-joyeuse-entree:
The Joyeuse Entrée was a famous charter of liberty granted to Brabant by Duke John III in 1354. John called the towns of the duchy to Louvain to announce the marriage of his daughter and heiress Jeanne to Wenceslaus of Luxemburg. To win their consent to the change of ruling house, he offered them wide concessions.

John died in 1355. Wenceslaus and Jeanne, at their state entry into Brussels, swore to keep the charter, which took its name from that occasion. By its terms the dukes promised to keep the duchy whole. They were to make no war, treaty, or tax without the consent of their subjects, voiced through the towns. All ducal councillors had to be native Brabanters. The charter became a model for other provinces and a shield for the liberties of the Netherlands. When Joseph II tried to sweep it away, Brabant rose in revolt and he yielded.
britannica-1911-kamptee: Kamptee, or Kamthi, is a town of British India in the Nagpur district of the Central Provinces. It stands below the meeting of the Kanhan, Pench, and Kolar rivers, 10 miles northeast of Nagpur by rail. Its population in 1901 was 38,888, falling steadily since 1881. Founded in 1821 as a military cantonment near Nagpur, it became a busy trade centre. Since the railway opened, trade has largely drifted to Nagpur, and the garrison has lately been cut down. It is well laid out, with wide roads and gardens.
britannica-1911-kankakee:
Kankakee is a city and the county seat of Kankakee county, Illinois, in the northeast of the state, on the Kankakee river, 56 miles south of Chicago. Its people numbered 13,595 in 1900, of whom 3346 were foreign born, and 13,986 in 1910. Three railways serve it, among them the Illinois Central. It holds the Eastern Hospital for the Insane, a state institution of 1879, a Catholic seminary, and a school of music.

At Bourbonnais Grove, three miles north, stands St Viateur's College, founded in 1868, with Notre Dame Academy near it. The city has a public library and four large parks, and in Court House Square a monument raised by public giving to the county's Civil War dead. Rock quarries work near by. Its factories make sewing machines, pianos and other instruments, foundry goods, farm tools, and furniture. The factory output of 1905 was valued at over two million dollars, more than three times the figure of 1900.
britannica-1911-kedgeree: Kedgeree, from the Hindostani khichri, is an Indian dish of boiled rice with various strongly flavoured additions. It comes in two kinds, white and yellow. The white is made with grain, onions, ghee, or clarified butter, cloves, pepper, and salt. The yellow kind counts eggs among its parts and takes its colour from turmeric. Among the poorer classes it is often made of rice and pulse alone, or of rice and beans. In European cookery the same name serves for a like dish, most often made with fish.
britannica-1911-kewanee:
Kewanee, a city in Henry County, Illinois, is the own subject of the city part of a shared page in the 1911 Britannica. The page first ends a note on Kew Gardens, then turns to the city. Kewanee lies in the north west of the state, north of Peoria. Two rail routes serve it, one a steam line and one an electric line. Its folk count for nineteen ten was nine thousand three hundred seven.

Works in town make boilers, wagons, farm tools, pipes, and gloves for work men. Shop goods of iron add to that list in the text. The worth of its shop goods rose by more than half in five years. First set down in eighteen thirty six by folk from Connecticut, it won city rule in eighteen ninety seven.
britannica-1911-laacher-see:
The Laacher See is a lake of Germany in the Prussian Rhine Province, 5 m. W. of Brohl on the Rhine and north of the village of Niedermendig. It fills what is thought to be a crater of the Eifel volcanic formation, as the pumice and basalt around it suggest. The lake lies 850 ft. above the sea, measures 5 m. in circumference and 160 ft. deep, and is ringed by high hills. Its water is sky blue, very cold and bitter, and with no natural outlet it rises and falls considerably.

On the western shore stands the Benedictine abbey of St Maria Laach, founded in 1093 by Henry II, count palatine of the Rhine. Its church dates from the 12th century and was restored in 1838. The abbey was abolished in 1802 and became a Prussian state demesne after the Napoleonic wars. Jesuits held it from 1863 to 1873, and Benedictines returned in 1892.
britannica-1911-lace-bark-tree: The lace-bark tree is a native of Jamaica, known botanically as Lagetta lintearia, from its native name lagetto. Its inner bark is made of many concentric layers of interlacing fibres that look like lace. Collars and other articles of clothing have been made from the fibre, which also serves for making whips. The tree belongs to the natural order Thymelaeaceae and is grown in hothouses in Britain.
britannica-1911-levee:
Levée, from a French word for raising, is an embankment that holds a river inside its channel, and this 1911 Britannica entry explains how such banks form. A big river such as the Mississippi carries a heavy load of mud and silt from its fast upper streams. Where the flow slows, it drops part of that load, most of all along its own sides. Over time the banks grow higher than the land around them, and the river ends up flowing above the plain.

In flood time, water spilling over drops still more silt on the outer slope, building a long low ridge called a natural levée. The entry warns that these ridges need close watching. If one breaks, the whole river can pour through the gap and flood the low country, as the Mississippi did near New Orleans in 1890.
britannica-1911-lime-tree:
Lime, or linden, covers trees of the genus Tilia. Sweet scent and honey fill their blooms. Some ten species grow across the north temperate zone. Linnaeus grouped the European kinds under one name, Tilia europaea. Three marked sub-kinds stand out in this account.

Small-leaved lime runs wild in England and most of Europe. Common lime is planted wide in Britain but is not wild there. Large-leaved lime comes to Britain only as a guest tree. Its leaves run four inches across at times. Great size marks old trees: one in Norfolk girthed sixteen yards. A famed linden at Neuenstadt gave that town its by-name. Spring green, flower scent that draws bees in swarms, and clear fall yellow mark the year. Avenues of limes close the praise.
britannica-1911-meeanee: Meeanee, also spelled Miani, is a brief place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names a village in Sind, in India, on the Indus river, six miles north of Hyderabad. Its count in 1901 was 962 people. The place is known for one event. On the seventeenth of February 1843 a battle was fought there. Sir Charles Napier, with only 2,800 men, broke the power of the mirs of Sind. The win led to the taking of Sind by Britain.
britannica-1911-murree:
Murree is a town and health resort of British India, in the Rawalpindi district of the Punjab. It stands 7,517 feet above the sea, about five hours by cart road from Rawalpindi town. It is also the start point for Kashmir. The houses stand on the top and sides of a rough ridge. From them the view runs over wooded hills and deep valleys, with farms, villages, and the snowy peaks of Kashmir beyond.

Murree held 1,844 people in 1901, but that count leaves out the summer guests, who may number 10,000. The guard force is most often three mountain batteries. Since 1877 the summer offices of the province have moved to Simla. The Murree brewery is one of the largest in India and the town's chief work. A school for the children of European soldiers also stands here.
britannica-1911-negaunee:
Negaunee is a city of Marquette county, Michigan, in the north of the upper peninsula, as this 1911 Britannica article describes it. It is built on a ridge called Iron Mountain, 1,564 feet above sea level, west by south of Marquette. Its people numbered 6,797 in 1904 and 8,460 in 1910, and three railways served it.

Under and near the city lie some of the most productive iron ore deposits in the state, and mining them is the chief trade of the place. Settlement began about 1870, and the city was chartered in 1873. The name is a Chippewa word meaning first, or he goes before. It is said to have been chosen at the wish of the Pioneer Iron Company as a match for the word pioneer.
britannica-1911-ogee:
Ogee is an architecture term defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names a moulding shaped with a double curve, one convex and one concave. The convex part is the uppermost of the two. The word is thought to be an English corruption of the French ogive, a diagonal groin rib.

The article gives the term's equals in other tongues. In Latin it is cyma reversa, in Italian gola, and in French cymaise. German builders call the same profile Kehlleisten. The name also passes to a form of arch. An ogee arch is made by the meeting of two contrasted ogees at the top. Readers are sent to the articles on mouldings and on the arch for fuller treatment of both uses.
britannica-1911-patel-framjee-nasarwanje:
Framjee Nasarwanjee Patel, a Parsee merchant and philanthropist who lived from 1804 to 1894, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1804, he had a sound education in his own tongue, with a smattering of English gained in Bombay. At age fifteen he entered on a business career in that city. Its pursuit proved so congenial that by 1827 he had worked his way to a partnership.

Banking facilities were then exceedingly scanty in Bombay for local men. Parsees with capital acted as bankers and brokers to the rising English firms of the port. The experience of Patel let him raise his compatriots to the level of independent merchants in a few years. In 1844 he founded a business house in which he was a partner with English members. When he retired in 1858 he had amassed a large competence from his trade.
britannica-1911-pawnee:
Pawnee names a tribe of North American Indians of Caddoan stock in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They once lived on the Platte river in Nebraska. Their own name for themselves, Skihiksihiks, is given as meaning men of men. The word Pawnee may come from their word for horn, tied to the stiff scalp lock they wore.

The article gives a short, hard history of loss. Their village was burned by the Delawares in 1823. Smallpox in 1838 is said to have killed two thousand of the tribe. By treaty in 1833 they gave up their land south of the Platte, and in 1858 nearly all the rest. They kept a strip on the Loup River until 1874. Then they moved to a reservation in Indian Territory, in what is now Oklahoma.
britannica-1911-pepper-tree:
The 1911 Britannica article on the pepper tree clears up a name. The tree has no real link with true pepper. It belongs to the cashew family. Its botanical name is Schinus Molle. That name comes from a Peruvian word. The tree is a native of tropical South America. It is grown in the open air in the south of Europe.

The article describes its finely cut leaves. The leaves are full of oil. The oil shows as specks when a leaf is held to the light. It leaps out when a leaf floats on water. The flowers are small and whitish. The fruit is pea-like. Its hot resin is used as a medicine in Peru. The resin acts much like mastic.
britannica-1911-spelling-bee:
A spelling bee is a match in which two sides compete in spelling words right. The custom is old, but it was revived in schools in the United States about eighteen seventy three. It spread fast through the country and to Great Britain. For a few years it was in great vogue, not just in schools. All classes and all ages took part in the craze.

Under the usual rules, a player who missed a word had to retire. The side with the most players left at the close won the match. Inter city and inter state matches were not unknown in the United States. The word bee, for a group met for joint work or play, came from America in colonial times. Husking bees and quilting bees are named as kin.
britannica-1911-suttee:
Suttee is the rite of the burn of a live widow on the pyre of her dead spouse, past some groups in India. The word comes from a term for a good wife or true wife. An old hymn book names the rite as an old use. Wise men have shown that a more old book was marred on point to back the rite.

That more old book seems to set a mere sign rite, where the widow was called back to life at the last hour. The true rite was rare in old days and no law book of old bids it. It grew strong past the sixth age.
britannica-1911-tallahassee:
Tallahassee is the capital of Florida and the county seat of Leon county. Its city entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies in the west part of the state, east of the Apalachicola river. It sits about midway by rail between Jacksonville and Pensacola cities.

The city stands fine on a hill, three hundred feet above the sea. Wide streets, well shaded by trees, run through the city plan. Chief buildings are the State Capitol, the Federal Building, and court house. Schools there serve women, and a state school trains Black students too. Its name is of Seminole origin and is said to mean tribal land.
britannica-1911-tallow-tree:
Tallow Tree is a short plant entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It explains a name used for more than one tree with rich, greasy seeds or fruit. The main tree named comes from China and is grown in India and other warm lands. Its seeds carry a thick white coat of fat.

The entry says that fat is used to make candles and soap and to dress cloth. It then names a second tree from Sierra Leone with the same common name. That tree bears a large fruit with a thick rind full of yellow grease. The note helps readers tell two plants apart that share one trade name.
britannica-1911-tegernsee:
Tegernsee is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a lake of Upper Bavaria in Germany. The lake lies 2,382 feet above the sea, thirty-four miles south of Munich. It is four miles long and some 235 feet deep. Its waters run out through the Mangfall into the Inn. High wooded hills ring its southern part.

The article turns to the shore and the village. Villages and villas line the banks, and the lake is a busy summer resort. The village of Tegernsee, on the east bank, had 1,742 people in 1905. It has a parish church of the fifteenth century and a ducal castle that was once a Benedictine monastery.
britannica-1911-tralee:
Tralee, the county town of Kerry, is placed in a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Leigh River, a mile from Tralee Bay. The Great Southern and Western line runs through the town. In 1901 its folk came to near ten thousand in count. A ship canal takes craft of two hundred tons to its quays.

Big ships drop their loads at Fenit, eight miles west. A pier and rail link tie that port to the town. Coal, iron, and timber come in, and grain goes out. Butter makes a large trade of the town as well. Rail spurs run to the sea resorts of the wild coast. Ardfert, four miles off, holds one of Ireland's oldest church sites.
britannica-1911-tree: Tree, in the wide sense, names all plants that grow with a lasting single woody trunk of some height, branching well above the ground. Its entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica notes the vague line between trees and shrubs, the latter being lower plants with several stems and bushy growth. Kindred words for tree or oak appear in Danish, Swedish, Greek, Welsh, and Sanskrit forms. The word also names pieces of wood used as frames or bars, as in a saddle tree or an axle tree.
britannica-1911-tuskegee:
Tuskegee is a town in Macon county in Alabama and the seat of that county. A 1911 Britannica entry gives its growth from 2170 people in 1900 to 2803 in 1910. A short rail line links it to the main road at Chehaw, five miles off. Local mills work cotton seed as the chief town product.

The town is best known for its schools, above all the Tuskegee Institute. Founded by state act in 1880, it opened in July 1881 under Booker Washington. Its aim was trade and farm training for Black students in the South. Gifts from Congress and from Andrew Carnegie helped the school grow fast.
britannica-1911-tyree:
Tyree is an island of the Inner Hebrides in Argyllshire, Scotland, with 2,192 people in 1901. It lies two miles south-west of Coll, with the small isle of Gunna in the channel between them. The island runs near 12 miles from north-east to south-west. Its width shifts from under a mile to over four miles. Carnan Mor, at 460 feet, is its high point, and it holds several lakes.

On Balephuill Bay, at the south-west point, stand the ruins of St Patrick's temple, plus duns and old chapels. Steamers from Oban call at the small harbour of Scarinish. The lone rock of Skerryvore, 14 miles to the south-west, belongs to the parish of Tyree. Its great lighthouse was built by Alan Stevenson from 1833 to 1843. The stone came from the granite pits of Hynish, at the island's south-east end.
britannica-1911-vendee:
Vendée is a coastal department of western France, and this 1911 Britannica entry describes its land and bounds. It was formed in 1790 out of Bas-Poitou and takes its name from a small tributary of the Sèvre Niortaise. The Atlantic bounds it on the west for ninety-three miles, and other departments close it on the north, east, and south. Its people numbered 442,777 in 1906, and its area runs to 2,708 square miles.

The islands of Yeu and Noirmoutier belong to it. Two rivers named Sèvre mark its north-east and south edges. The land falls into three parts: woodland, plain, and marsh. The woodland covers most of the department and holds its highest point at 748 feet. Its open fields ringed by trees, the entry notes, gave cover to the Vendeans in the civil war at the end of the eighteenth century.
britannica-1911-yankee:
Yankee is a slang name for a citizen of the New England states in America, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. In loose European use it is applied to any citizen of the United States. British soldiers used it of their foes in the War of Independence. In the Civil War the Confederates used it of Federal troops and of the North in general.

Much ink has been spent on where the name came from, the text notes. One early source calls it a cant word at Cambridge in Massachusetts as early as 1713, used for excellence. He holds that it renders the native pronunciation of English or Anglais, applied by the Massachusetts Indians to English settlers. A Scots word yankie, meaning sharp or clever, is set out as a rival source in the account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acanthus-titu:
Acanthus, a Macedonian titular see on the Strymonic Gulf, is now Erisso. Herodotus, book seven, records Xerxes praising its inhabitants for their zeal in his cause. That classical praise gives the small see a place in Greek history well before its Christian record.

The ruins of a large curving mole jutting far into the sea still stood in the early nineteenth century. The entry cites Smith's dictionary of Greek and Roman geography and Leake's travels in northern Greece, and its brevity matches a see known chiefly by site, ancient praise, and surviving harbour works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-augus:
Antoine-Augustin Touttée, a French Benedictine monk of the Maurist reform, lived from 1677 to 1718. After study with the Oratorians at Riom, he took vows at Vendôme and taught philosophy and theology at three abbeys. He then withdrew to Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris to prepare a new edition of Saint Cyril of Jerusalem.

His Greek text with a Latin translation appeared after his death in 1720, edited by Prudent Maran. Three learned essays on Cyril's life, writings, and teaching open the volume. At the time it stood as the standard edition, and the entry presents Touttée as a quiet scholar whose one great book outlived him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bersabee:
Bersabee, or Beersheba, a town at Palestine's southern edge, receives a full entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Through most of Hebrew history it marked the south as Dan marked the north, so that from Dan to Bersabee meant the whole land. After the northern kingdom's fall, the phrase shifted to other southern bounds.

Its name draws long debate, with wells, oaths, and seven sacred things all proposed, and two Genesis stories giving rival accounts of its naming by Abraham and Isaac. The entry weighs Hebrew roots, wells, and patriarchal tales. It is a place-name study as much as a town history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-berthold-of-c:
Berthold of Chiemsee, a German bishop and theological writer, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. His true name was Berthold Pürstinger, born at Salzburg in 1465 and dead at Saalfelden in 1543. Trained in civil and church law, he served as master of the chamber to Salzburg's archbishop and became Bishop of Chiemsee in 1508.

Residing at Salzburg as coadjutor to the archbishop, he wrote against the Lutheran reform, defending Catholic teaching in clear German prose. He resigned his see in 1525 and spent his last years writing. The entry presents a bishop-scholar answering the Reformation from within the old Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cedar-tree:
The cedar tree of the Bible, Hebrew érez, Greek kedros, Latin cedrus, usually means the celebrated cedar of Lebanon. The name can cover several conifers, but in most passages the Lebanon cedar is meant. It is a tree of high stature, raised high above every other tree in the land, as Ezekiel and Isaiah describe it. Its wood and its height made it a natural image of majesty.

In a few passages, though, the Lebanon cedar cannot be meant. In Leviticus and Numbers the wood had to be one the Israelites could readily find during their desert wandering. A juniper of the Arabah, Juniperus Phoenicea, whose wood is also aromatic, is the likelier tree. The article weighs each passage in turn to decide which tree the text intends.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-miche:
An entry on Charles Michel de l'Epée, the French priest who invented a sign alphabet for teaching deaf people and founded their schooling. Born at Versailles in 1712, he studied theology but was refused ordination for declining to condemn Jansenism. After qualifying in law, he was ordained by the Bishop of Troyes and returned to Paris, where he took on the education of two deaf sisters.

De l'Epée built a set of conventional signs into a full alphabet, teaching through the eye what hearing children learn through the ear. He opened a school at his own expense and outdid earlier teachers such as Pereira, Bulwer, and Wallis. His method was later replaced by lip-reading, in which pupils watch and copy lip and tongue movements. The entry credits his sign system with laying the foundations of organised instruction of the deaf. He died in Paris in 1789.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cornelius-van:
Gregory Cleary's entry treats Cornelius van Zierikzee, born at Zierikzee, a Zeeland town in Holland, about 1405, died 21 February 1462. The Franciscan Rule's strict observance, upheld and propagated through Italy by Saint Bernardine of Siena and Saint John Capistran, had early entered Germany. At twenty Cornelius entered the Franciscan Order in Cologne province, then including most of the Netherlands. That province was famous for its members' number and sanctity, including several Scotsmen educated at Continental universities.

Bernardine's revival of Franciscan life no doubt reached King James I of Scotland, whose poetic spirit harmonized with the Franciscan ideal. In 1436 the king asked the order's superiors for Friars of the Observance to be sent into Scotland. The Scottish Franciscans enjoyed a great European reputation for adhering most conscientiously and strictly to the order's poverty and austerity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cree:
An ethnological entry introduces the Cree, the greatest and most important Indian tribe of Canada, part of the great Algonquin stock and close kin to the Ojibwa. Before confinement to reservations, their bands held vast territory around Lakes Winnipeg and Manitoba and the lower Red and Saskatchewan rivers, and east toward Hudson Bay.

Known to Jesuit missionaries about 1650, the Cree pushed onto the open plains once English trading posts supplied firearms, driving the Blackfeet before them and warring with the Tinneh tribes. A smallpox epidemic in 1781 cut their numbers sharply. The entry covers their alliances, wars, physique, and customs, and notes their generally friendly relations with both French and English.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-decree:
A canon law entry defines a decree, from Latin for I judge, as an order or law made by superior authority for others' direction. In church use it takes several senses. Any papal Bull, Brief, or Motu Proprio counts as a decree, as a legislative act of the Holy Father. Pope Siricius already cites the general decrees of Liberius.

Roman Congregations issue decrees within their jurisdiction, and provinces and dioceses issue them in synods. The word also names collections of church law, above all Gratian's Decree. Papal and council decrees bind universally, while Trent first applied the term indiscriminately to rulings on faith and reform. Congregation decrees bind certainly in the case judged, but whether they bind as general law depends on whether they enlarge or merely explain the law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-edou:
Francois Edouard Joachim Coppee, born at Paris on 26 January 1842 and dead on 23 May 1908, was a French poet, dramatist, and novelist of the Parnassian school. His father, a War Department clerk, modelled a true Christian life. Francois studied at Lycee Saint-Louis until straitened family means forced him out before graduating to help support them. He finished his education by private study in long hours at the Sainte-Genevieve Library after hard days' work.

Joining the Parnassian poets in 1863, he published his first verses, Le Reliquaire, in 1866, followed by Intimites, and his first play, Le Passant, in 1869. Through Princesse Mathilde he became assistant librarian of the Senate, then librarian of the Comedie Francaise from 1871 to 1885. He won the Legion of Honour in 1876 and entered the French Academy in 1884.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-von:
Friedrich von Spee, a Jesuit poet born on the Rhine in 1591, wrote the book that first broke the witch trials in Germany. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1610, taught at Trier, Würzburg, and other cities, and was ordained in 1622. An attempt on his life at Peine in 1629 failed. He died at Trier in 1635 from sickness caught while nursing the suffering in a hospital.

His Cautio Criminalis, printed without his name in 1631, laid bare the rack, the forced confessions, and the unjust judges of the trials. Spee sought reform rather than instant abolition, yet his book ended witch burning at Mainz and pointed the way to its slow end elsewhere. His sacred songs, the Trutznachtigall, still rank high among seventeenth-century religious lyrics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabriel-augus:
Gabriel-Auguste Daubrée, a French geologist born at Metz in 1814, founded experimental geology by making rocks in the laboratory. Trained in mining engineering at the École Polytechnique, he entered government service in 1834 and published on Scandinavian ore deposits, winning the notice of Berzelius. A Strasburg chair from 1849 gave him the laboratory his experiments needed.

Daubrée made minerals by art, tested superheated steam, grinding, pressure, and strain in mountain building, and studied the hot springs of Plombières in detail. Admitted to the Academy of Sciences in 1861, he taught geology at Paris's Natural History Museum and later directed the School of Mines. A mineral in meteoric iron, daubréelite, still bears his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-galilee:
Galilee, the native land of Jesus, is where he began his ministry, worked many wonders, and chose his apostles. The Hebrew name comes from a word for circle or district, first marking the part of Naphtali around Kedesh, a city of refuge. Solomon's gift of twenty northern towns to Hiram of Tyre also bore the name, and Isaiah called the mixed land Galilee of the Nations.

By New Testament times Galilee, with Samaria and Judea, divided western Palestine, split by a ridge into Upper and Lower halves. Josephus counted 204 thriving villages and fifteen walled towns there, on soil rich enough for a great people. Today its folk are few and scattered, though Safed in the north and Nazareth in the south still anchor the old land.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gilbert-de-la:
Gilbert de la Porrée, also called Gilbertus Porretanus, was a philosopher, theologian, and Bishop of Poitiers, born at Poitiers in 1076 and dead in 1154. He studied under Hilary at Poitiers, Bernard at Chartres, and Anselm at Laon, where he likely first met Abelard. He taught philosophy at Chartres for about fifteen years before becoming a bishop in 1142. A Catholic Encyclopedia article places him at the heart of early scholastic thought.

His Liber Sex Principiorum explained Aristotle's last six categories and served as a school textbook for three centuries. His commentary on Boethius on the Trinity drew fire for its doctrine of universals, and two archdeacons carried the charge to Eugene III. St. Bernard opposed him at Paris in 1147 and Reims in 1148, yet the dispute ended without a firm verdict. Later readers have read his realism in several ways, from ontological to moderate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-klee:
Rhineland theologian Heinrich Klee, born at Münstermaifeld in 1800, carried sound Catholic doctrine into rationalist Bonn and on to Möhler's chair at Munich, dying within a year of the move. A Mainz seminarian at seventeen, professor of exegesis and history there in 1824, he took Bonn's chair in 1829 over Freiburg's, facing Hermesian dominance with tact, genial lectures, and learned books.

Ten years at Bonn teaching dogmatic and moral theology, history of dogma, and exegesis won him influence. Munich called him in 1839 after the Cologne archbishop's clash with the Hermesians. His Catholic Dogmatics in three volumes ran through four editions, his history of dogma in two. Commentaries on John, Romans, and Hebrews preceded a posthumous ethics, though views on the soul's origin and unbaptized infants drew criticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-and-jul:
Belgian brothers Henri and Jules Desclée founded a monastery and a printing house that reshaped Catholic art and chant. When Kulturkampf exiles from Beuron sought refuge in Belgium, the brothers, Jules a former papal Zouave captain, gave them a Namur estate. There Baron Béthune built Maredsous in pure thirteenth-century Gothic, its 120 monks devoted to liturgy, study, and teaching.

A college and technical school followed in 1882 and 1902, and in 1882 the brothers founded at Tournai the Society of St. John the Evangelist to restore medieval beauty to liturgical books, using English craftsmen at first. Their plainchant editions, following Pothier and Solesmes, grounded the Vatican edition Pius X imposed, and a sister Society of St. Augustine spread the same art to religious books and images.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-see:
The Holy See, from the Latin Sancta Sedes or Holy Chair, takes its name from Rome's bishops' enthronement ceremony. It must not be confused with the ancient gestatorial chair in St. Peter's apse, venerated as the Chair of Peter. In general use it means the supreme pastor of the church's actual seat, or residence, plus the authorities forming the central administration.

In canonical and diplomatic use it matches Apostolic See, Holy Apostolic See, Roman Church, and Roman Curia. The word sedes, chair, first marked churches founded by apostles, then the great patriarchal sees: Rome, Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem, and Constantinople. Rome was expressly called the first see properly so named, and the entry traces the title from those roots.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-year-of-:
The Holy Year of Jubilee takes its name most probably from the Hebrew jobel, a ram's horn blown to proclaim the celebration. Through Greek and Latin forms the word blended with jubilo, to shout, giving the forms jubilatio and jubilaeum used across Europe. The idea of rejoicing thus clings to the word from its roots.

For Israelites the jubilee was a year of remission and universal pardon. Leviticus commands sanctifying the fiftieth year and proclaiming remission to all inhabitants of the land. Every seventh year was holy for rest, but the year after seven cycles carried special solemnity. Talmudists later disputed whether the jubilee fell in the forty-ninth or fiftieth year, since the latter would set two sabbatical years in a row.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-metropolis-ti:
Metropolis, a titular episcopal see and suffragan of Ephesus, lay between Ephesus and Smyrna, one hundred and twenty stadia, nearly fourteen miles, from Ephesus, by Strabo's account, who praises its famed wines. Le Quien names only two bishops: Marcellinus at Chalcedon in 451 and John at the pseudo-Council of Photius in 878. But the Notitiae Episcopatuum show the diocese still alive in the fourteenth century.

Metropolis is now wholly destroyed, its ruins visible at Tratsa in the Torbali district of Smyrna province, close to the Caystrus River. The nearby village of Torbali was built with stone from ancient Metropolis. At Tratsa one may still see part of its wall, its theatre, and its acropolis of huge blocks, with olive groves dotted with architectural ruins. This Metropolis must not be confused with two namesakes, one in Phrygia and one in Thessaly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-milwaukee:
Milwaukee, erected as a diocese on 28 November 1843 and raised to an archbishopric on 12 February 1875, covers seventeen Wisconsin counties, an area of 9,321 square miles. The city stands picturesquely on Milwaukee Bay, on Lake Michigan's eastern shore, its name coming from an Algonquin dialect word meaning Good Land. Catholicism there is first mentioned in the Catholic Almanac of 1840.

In 1841 Bishop Lefevre of Detroit first visited Milwaukee, with Father Martin Kundig, whose name is bound up with the diocese's early growth. In 1843 the Fifth Provincial Council of Baltimore petitioned Rome to make Milwaukee a see and appoint John Martin Henni, born at Obersaxen, Switzerland, in 1805, as its first bishop. The archdiocese's Catholic population was estimated at about 238,000.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-osee:
Osee, or Hosea, Beeri's son, counts among the Minor Prophets of the northern kingdom of Israel, which he calls simply the land. He names its king our king and knows its towns well, while he speaks of Judah seldom and never names Jerusalem. His ministry is dated by the book's title from about 750 to 725 before Christ, under Jeroboam II in Israel and four kings of Judah.

Judged by his own allusions, his years run closer to 750 to 735, beside the closing years of Amos and the first appearance of Isaiah. Jeroboam's outward splendour masked fast political and religious decay, and kings fell in quick murders. The book falls in two parts. Chapters 1 to 3 use his marriage to Gomer as a figure of faithless Israel, while chapters 4 to 14 denounce idolatry and foretell ruin, with mercy held out at the end.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-petitions-to-:
Petitions to the Holy See were the written road to every favour Rome alone could grant: faculties, indults, dispensations, and the like. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that a petition goes to the pope himself, normally through a congregation of the Roman Curia, though Pius X's constitution let any private person approach directly. Commendatory letters from one's bishop help, and are often required, and a trustworthy Roman agent may handle the matter in person.

Form mattered as much as substance. The petition belonged on a double foolscap or large quarto sheet, its text running page to page like a printed book with no blank leaf between. Latin, Italian, and French were the Curia's official tongues, though English, German, Spanish, and Portuguese stood authorized, and Latin best suited bishops, clergy, and sacramental matters. Every petition opened with the words Beatissime Pater, Most Holy Father.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scillium-titu:
Scillium, a titular see in Africa Proconsularis suffragan of Carthage, may properly be written Scilium, with a real name of Scilli or Scili. On 17 July 180 six martyrs suffered there for the faith, and later a basilica where Augustine preached was dedicated to them near Douar esh-Shott. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia chases a name through Greek and Latin sources.

A later addition to the Greek Acts calls the martyrs natives of Ischle in Numidia, a Greek rendering of Scillium. The primitive Carthage calendar already lists them on 16 Kalends of August as the Scilitans. The Greek compiler may have meant Numidian country rather than the province, placing Scillium in Proconsular Numidia. An epitaph at Simitthu reads Iscilitana, but whether Scillium lay near it, the entry admits, cannot be finally settled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sea-of-galile:
The Sea of Galilee bears many names. John's Gospel calls it the sea of Tiberias, Luke the lake of Gennesaret, Numbers and Joshua the sea of Chinnereth, Maccabees the water of Gennesar, and Pliny the Lake of Tarichea. It lies in the Jordan gorge 682 feet below the Mediterranean. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia maps a lake of many names.

An irregular oval nearly thirteen miles long, it reaches about seven and a half miles at its widest near the northern end. Mountains wall it east and west. The eastern range, a uniform wall 2,000 feet high, slopes steeply to within half a mile of shore. The western hills, lower and more broken, draw near the water northward. At the north-west corner the shore widens into a triangular plain of marvellous fertility running four miles east.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-aengus-the:
St. Aengus the Culdee was an Irish saint of the last quarter of the eighth century, honoured above all as author of the Felire, the festology of the saints. This entry follows a boy born near Clonengh and schooled at St. Fintan's monastery there, who became a hermit at Disert-beagh on the Nore, where tradition says he communed with angels.

His love of prayer and solitude earned him the name Culdee, Ceile De, servant of God. And, finding his first hermitage too near Clonenagh and its passing students, he moved eight miles off to a lonelier place, the Desert of Aengus. Where he raised a small oratory among the Dysert Hills. The entry preserves a saint whose calendar of feasts outlived his solitude.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tegernsee:
Tegernsee, called Tegrinseo in 817 and Tegernsee in 754, was a celebrated Benedictine abbey of Bavaria, important for early medieval civilization. It stood on the Tyrol road by Lake Tegern, southeast of Munich. Tegern meant large in Old High German, so the name means large lake. Counts Adalbert and Otkar of Warngau founded it in 746, not 719 as once supposed, near an existing Church of Our Saviour. It was consecrated and occupied in 754.

The founding family was the Huosi, not the Agilolfingers, and the tale of St Othmar colonizing it is legendary. Magyar raids cloud its first decades, but one fact is firm. The founders won St Quirinus's relics from Pope Paul I, not Zacharias, and brought them from Rome in the later eighth century. The first abbot, Adalbert, appears in a charter of 804 as recently dead, and had attended the Synod of Dingolfing in 770. The entry follows the abbey's long history to 1429.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tennessee:
Tennessee lies between 35° and 36°30' north and 81°37' and 90°38' west. It stretches 432 miles east to west and 109 miles at its widest, covering 43,022 square miles. It touches eight states, more than any other state except Missouri. Its rivers are unmatched in number and excellence. The Mississippi washes its west, while the Tennessee and Cumberland furnish cheap transport for soil and mine products. The state holds eight great natural divisions.

The Appalachian Unakis rise on the east border, with peaks above 6,000 feet. Westward lies the east Tennessee valley of ridges and minor valleys. Then comes the Cumberland table-land, a plateau 2,000 feet high with thin sandy soil but vast coal and iron beneath, covering 5,100 square miles. Beyond it the highlands average 1,000 feet, with rolling hills and wide valleys of varying fertility. At their centre sits the great central basin, the Garden of Tennessee, covering 5,450 square miles of very productive soil.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-apostolic:
A metaphor turned into a title is unpacked here: the Apostolic See, the seat of authority in the Roman Church that carries on the work of Peter, chief of the Apostles. In general use, an apostolic see means any see founded by an Apostle and holding its founder's authority. Rome alone kept that claim intact after heresy, schism, and barbarian violence swept other claimant churches away.

By the fourth century Rome already stood as the Apostolic See par excellence, honoured in East as well as West. Antioch, Alexandria, and Jerusalem receive their due in the survey, but the entry explains why the phrase became Rome's proper name. It closes by tracing how that authority was understood across the early centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-d-arcy:
Thomas d'Arcy McGee, editor, politician and poet, was born at Carlingford, Ireland, in 1825 and assassinated at Ottawa in 1868. Emigrating to America at seventeen, he won work on the Boston Pilot after a speech on repealing the Union, and O'Connell praised his early writing. Back in Dublin he joined the Young Ireland paper Nation, served as secretary of the Irish Confederation, and fled to America disguised as a priest after the rising of 1848.

In Canada he changed course entirely, entering Parliament and pressing for British supremacy as warmly as he had once pressed for revolution. Confederation owed much to his drive, and his attacks on Fenian groups made him hated by former allies. His poems and histories, including a History of Ireland in 1862, kept his literary name alive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trincomalee:
A diocese in Ceylon, suffragan of Colombo, created in 1893 by dividing the diocese of Jaffna. It covers the whole eastern province and the district of Tamankuduwa, and out of 186,251 people counts 8,773 Catholics, with 28 churches and chapels served by Jesuit fathers and two missionaries Apostolic.

Candidates for the priesthood are sent to the Kandy seminary, and the diocese runs fifty-five schools with 2,523 pupils. A convent of the Sisters of St. Joseph of Cluny, with five sisters, conducts an orphanage, and the bishop, Charles Lavigne, a Jesuit consecrated in 1887, resides at Trincomalee.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-j-har:
William J. Hardee was an American soldier and convert who wrote the army's rifle tactics manual. Born at Savannah, Georgia, in 1817, he died at Wytheville, Virginia, in 1873. He graduated from West Point in 1838, served with the second dragoons in the Florida Indian war, and in 1839 trained at the French school of Saint Maur with the French cavalry. Back in America he served in the West and rose to dragoon captain in September 1844.

Hardee fought with distinction in the Mexican War, then prepared a tactics manual finished in 1856 and became commandant of cadets at West Point. His United States Rifle and Light Infantry Tactics of 1856 borrowed chiefly from French sources rather than breaking new ground.
